\begin{corollary}[First spectral-approximation entry rule from prism readout]
\label{cor:first-spectral-approximation-entry-rule-from-prism-readout}
Whenever a later argument in the present public v3.23.0 release line uses only a reduced prism-readout sector on the retained carrier surface, it is sufficient to treat the resulting output angles or ordered boundary positions as a first spectral approximation layer. In particular, the wavelength-ordered boundary data may be used as a first approximation probe of the effective refractive profile
\[
  n_{\mathrm{eff}}(\lambda)
\]
without reopening a stronger global optical theory of the full crystal--shadow architecture.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
This is the operational reformulation of Lemma~\ref{lem:first-prism-readout-lemma-on-the-retained-carrier-surface}. The lemma already isolates the precise point at which ordinary prism-type wavelength ordering is available on the retained carrier surface, so the corresponding output angles or ordered boundary positions may be used as first spectral approximation data.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Status of the first residual spectral-diagnostic step in v3.23]
\label{rem:status-of-the-first-residual-spectral-diagnostic-step-in-v323}
The present public v3.23.0 release line still does \emph{not} claim a full inverse spectral theory of the crystal--shadow architecture. What it now does support, however, is one first residual-diagnostic layer: once a reduced prism-readout sector and measured output data are both available, the difference between measured and modeled boundary readout may already be organized as a diagnostic signal for boundary, carrier, and defect contributions.
\end{remark}

\begin{definition}[Prism-readout residual profile]
\label{def:prism-readout-residual-profile}
Let a reduced prism-readout sector be given in the sense of Definition~\ref{def:reduced-prism-readout-sector}, and let
\[
\delta_{\mathrm{mod}}(\lambda)
\]
denote the modeled prism-type output angle produced by the corresponding effective refractive profile
\[
n_{\mathrm{eff}}(\lambda)
\]
on the retained carrier surface. Let
\[
\delta_{\mathrm{meas}}(\lambda)
\]
denote measured output-angle data for the same wavelength channel. The \emph{prism-readout residual profile} is the wavelength-indexed discrepancy
\[
\Delta_{\delta}(\lambda)
:=
\delta_{\mathrm{meas}}(\lambda)-\delta_{\mathrm{mod}}(\lambda).
\]
When refractive-index data are available instead of output angles, the corresponding effective-index residual is
\[
\Delta_n(\lambda)
:=
n_{\mathrm{meas}}(\lambda)-n_{\mathrm{eff}}(\lambda).
\]
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[First residual spectral-diagnostic lemma]
\label{lem:first-residual-spectral-diagnostic-lemma}
Let a reduced prism-readout sector be given on the retained carrier surface, together with a prism-readout residual profile
\[
\Delta_{\delta}(\lambda)
\]
or an effective-index residual profile
\[
\Delta_n(\lambda).
\]
Assume that the argument stays inside the reduced prism-readout layer of Lemma~\ref{lem:first-prism-readout-lemma-on-the-retained-carrier-surface}. Then the following first diagnostic reading is admissible:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=2em,label=(\roman*)]
  \item if the residual is approximately wavelength-independent across the working visible sector, it may be read first as a boundary/wedge calibration discrepancy rather than as evidence for a second carrier;
  \item if the residual varies smoothly and monotonically with wavelength while preserving the ordinary ordering of the spectrum, it may be read first as mismatch in the effective refractive profile of the retained carrier, rather than as a failure of the reduced optical sector itself;
  \item if the residual shows localized spikes, abnormal broadening, splitting, or branch-like irregularity, it may be read first as defect-face contamination, unresolved anisotropy, or residual multi-branch visible readout effects still subordinate to the retained carrier description.
\end{enumerate}
Thus the first spectral residual need not be treated merely as numerical error: it may already be organized as a structural diagnostic signal for boundary, carrier-profile, and defect-side corrections.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
By Lemma~\ref{lem:first-prism-readout-lemma-on-the-retained-carrier-surface}, the reduced prism-readout sector already compresses the optical readout to one retained carrier surface with an effective refractive profile and ordinary prism-type wavelength ordering. Therefore the residual between measured and modeled output should first be interpreted inside that same reduced sector before postulating any new foundational carrier. A wavelength-independent shift changes the overall angular output without changing the relative spectral ordering, so the first admissible reading is boundary or wedge calibration error. A smooth wavelength-dependent drift changes the effective dispersion profile while preserving the same retained carrier picture, so the first admissible reading is mismatch in the carrier-side refractive response. By contrast, localized spikes, broadening, or branch-like irregularity are precisely the kinds of visible effects expected when defect-face contamination, unresolved anisotropy, or incomplete branch suppression is still present in the readout layer. Hence the stated three-way residual reading is structurally admissible.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[First spectral-fit entry rule from prism residuals]
\label{cor:first-spectral-fit-entry-rule-from-prism-residuals}
Whenever measured optical data are available for a reduced prism-readout sector in the present public v3.23.0 release line, it is sufficient to begin with the prism-readout residual profile
\[
\Delta_{\delta}(\lambda)
\quad\text{or}\quad
\Delta_n(\lambda)
\]
and classify the first discrepancy into boundary-type, carrier-profile-type, or defect/readout-type correction, before attempting any stronger global optical inversion. In particular, the first fitting layer may be organized around the effective refractive profile
\[
n_{\mathrm{eff}}(\lambda)
\]
and its residuals rather than around a full new optical theory of the whole crystal--shadow architecture.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
This is the operational reformulation of Lemma~\ref{lem:first-residual-spectral-diagnostic-lemma}. The lemma already isolates the precise point at which optical residuals may be used as structured diagnostic data rather than as undifferentiated fitting error.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Status of the first parametric spectral-fit layer in v3.23]
\label{rem:status-of-the-first-parametric-spectral-fit-layer-in-v323}
The present public v3.23.0 release line still does \emph{not} claim a final physically unique refractive law for the full crystal--shadow architecture. What it now does support, however, is one first parametric fit layer on the reduced prism-readout sector: a small family of wavelength laws may already be used as effective carrier-side dispersion templates and compared directly with measured optical data.
\end{remark}

\begin{definition}[First effective carrier-dispersion fit ansatz]
\label{def:first-effective-carrier-dispersion-fit-ansatz}
In the reduced prism-readout sector, the first parametric carrier-side fit ansatz is the Cauchy-type effective refractive profile
\[
n_{\mathrm{eff}}(\lambda)
=
A + \frac{B}{\lambda^2} + \frac{C}{\lambda^4},
\]
where:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=2em,label=(\roman*)]
  \item $A$ is the coarse carrier baseline level;
  \item $B$ is the first wavelength-dispersion coefficient;
  \item $C$ is the first curvature/refinement coefficient of the reduced visible readout law.
\end{enumerate}
When needed, the corresponding modeled prism angle is written
\[
\delta_{\mathrm{mod}}(\lambda;A,B,C).
\]
\end{definition}

\begin{proposition}[First parametric spectral-fit principle]
\label{prop:first-parametric-spectral-fit-principle}
Let measured output-angle data
\[
\delta_{\mathrm{meas}}(\lambda_i)
\]
be given on a finite visible wavelength grid $\{\lambda_i\}_{i=1}^N$ for a reduced prism-readout sector. Let
\[
\delta_{\mathrm{mod}}(\lambda_i;A,B,C)
\]
be the modeled output-angle data induced by the effective carrier-dispersion fit ansatz of Definition~\ref{def:first-effective-carrier-dispersion-fit-ansatz}. Then the parameter triple
\[
(A,B,C)
\]
may already be used as a first structured fit layer with the following diagnostic reading:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=2em,label=(\roman*)]
  \item the fitted baseline term $A$ controls the carrier-side mean refractive level and therefore the first global angular placement of the spectrum;
  \item the fitted coefficient $B$ controls the first visible wavelength ordering slope and therefore the dominant red-to-blue spread;
  \item the fitted coefficient $C$ controls the first curvature correction and therefore the first higher-order bending of the spectral spacing;
  \item the post-fit residual
  \[
  \Delta_{\delta}^{\mathrm{fit}}(\lambda_i)
  :=
  \delta_{\mathrm{meas}}(\lambda_i)-\delta_{\mathrm{mod}}(\lambda_i;A,B,C)
  \]
  may then be fed into the residual diagnostic layer of Lemma~\ref{lem:first-residual-spectral-diagnostic-lemma}.
\end{enumerate}
Thus the first optical fitting step may already be organized as a carrier-baseline / dispersion-slope / curvature decomposition before any stronger global inversion is attempted.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Definition~\ref{def:first-effective-carrier-dispersion-fit-ansatz} supplies a three-parameter effective refractive profile whose terms already separate a wavelength-independent baseline contribution from the first and second visible dispersion corrections. In a prism-readout sector, the modeled boundary angle is determined by the effective refractive response together with the fixed wedge geometry, so changes in $A$ primarily shift the coarse refractive level, changes in $B$ primarily alter the leading wavelength ordering, and changes in $C$ primarily alter the first curvature correction of the spacing. Once these parameters are fitted to measured data, the remaining discrepancy is exactly a residual profile of the kind introduced in Definition~\ref{def:prism-readout-residual-profile}. Therefore the fitted three-parameter law gives a first structured fit layer, and the remaining discrepancy may be read through the residual diagnostic layer rather than treated as undifferentiated numerical error.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[First carrier-fit workflow for optical data]
\label{cor:first-carrier-fit-workflow-for-optical-data}
Whenever measured prism-type optical data are available in the present public v3.23.0 release line, it is sufficient to proceed in the following first workflow:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=2em,label=(\roman*)]
  \item fit the reduced carrier-side ansatz
  \[
  n_{\mathrm{eff}}(\lambda)=A+B/\lambda^2+C/\lambda^4;
  \]
  \item compute the modeled output angles
  \[
  \delta_{\mathrm{mod}}(\lambda_i;A,B,C);
  \]
  \item form the post-fit residual profile
  \[
  \Delta_{\delta}^{\mathrm{fit}}(\lambda_i);
  \]
  \item classify the remaining discrepancy by the residual spectral-diagnostic layer as primarily boundary-type, carrier-profile-type, or defect/readout-type.
\end{enumerate}
A finer reopening is required only when one wants to go beyond the first effective carrier-dispersion template and derive a stronger global optical law of the full crystal--shadow architecture.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
This is the operational reformulation of Proposition~\ref{prop:first-parametric-spectral-fit-principle}. The proposition already isolates the precise point at which the first three-parameter carrier-side fit can be used as the entry layer for measured optical data.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Status of the first spectral-calibration step in v3.23]
\label{rem:status-of-the-first-spectral-calibration-step-in-v323}
The present public v3.23.0 release line still does \emph{not} claim a final unique inverse solution for the full optical sector of the crystal--shadow architecture. What it now does support, however, is one first calibration step for the reduced carrier-dispersion law: under fixed wedge geometry and a reduced prism-readout sector, the three-parameter carrier-side ansatz may already be anchored by finite spectral data.
\end{remark}

\begin{proposition}[First three-parameter spectral-calibration principle]
\label{prop:first-three-parameter-spectral-calibration-principle}
Let
\[
n_{\mathrm{eff}}(\lambda)=A+\frac{B}{\lambda^2}+\frac{C}{\lambda^4}
\]
be the effective carrier-dispersion fit ansatz of Definition~\ref{def:first-effective-carrier-dispersion-fit-ansatz}, and assume a fixed prism-type wedge geometry in a reduced prism-readout sector. Let measured output-angle data
\[
\delta_{\mathrm{meas}}(\lambda_i)
\]
be given at at least three distinct visible wavelengths
\[
\lambda_1,\lambda_2,\lambda_3.
\]
Then the parameter triple
\[
(A,B,C)
\]
may already be calibrated in a first structured sense from these data, subject to the reduced optical model, with the following reading:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=2em,label=(\roman*)]
  \item the coarse mean placement of the measured spectrum fixes the baseline scale for $A$;
  \item the dominant red-to-blue spread fixes the first dispersion scale for $B$;
  \item the deviation from purely affine wavelength ordering fixes the first curvature scale for $C$.
\end{enumerate}
If more than three wavelength channels are available, then $(A,B,C)$ may be chosen by least-squares or analogous residual minimization and the remaining discrepancy passed to the residual diagnostic layer.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
In the reduced prism-readout sector, the wedge geometry is fixed and the optical response is compressed to the three-parameter effective refractive profile of Definition~\ref{def:first-effective-carrier-dispersion-fit-ansatz}. Therefore the modeled output-angle family
\[
\delta_{\mathrm{mod}}(\lambda_i;A,B,C)
\]
depends only on three carrier-side parameters. Distinct visible wavelengths sample distinct values of the basis functions
\[
1,\qquad \lambda^{-2},\qquad \lambda^{-4}.
\]
Hence three distinct wavelength channels already provide the first minimal calibration layer for these three carrier-side contributions, while additional channels overdetermine the fit and allow residual minimization. The qualitative reading of the three parameters follows directly from their roles in the ansatz: $A$ sets the coarse baseline refractive level, $B$ sets the leading dispersion slope, and $C$ sets the first curvature correction. Therefore the stated calibration reading is admissible.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[First identifiability rule for optical fit parameters]
\label{cor:first-identifiability-rule-for-optical-fit-parameters}
Whenever a later argument in the present public v3.23.0 release line uses the first reduced carrier-dispersion fit ansatz on a fixed prism geometry, it is sufficient to treat three distinct visible wavelength channels as the first minimal identifiability threshold for the parameter triple
\[
(A,B,C),
\]
while any additional channels are used to diagnose model mismatch via the post-fit residual profile. A finer reopening is required only when one wants to replace the three-parameter ansatz itself by a stronger global optical law.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
This is the operational reformulation of Proposition~\ref{prop:first-three-parameter-spectral-calibration-principle}. The proposition already isolates the precise point at which the three fit parameters become minimally identifiable in the reduced optical sector.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Status of the first overdetermined spectral-consistency step in v3.23]
\label{rem:status-of-the-first-overdetermined-spectral-consistency-step-in-v323}
The present public v3.23.0 release line still does \emph{not} claim that every optical data set can already be decided by the first three-parameter ansatz alone. What it now does support, however, is one first overdetermined consistency test: when more than the minimal three visible channels are available, the reduced prism-readout sector may already be checked for self-consistency against real data before any stronger optical law is introduced.
\end{remark}

\begin{proposition}[First overdetermined spectral-consistency principle]
\label{prop:first-overdetermined-spectral-consistency-principle}
Let measured prism-type output-angle data
\[
\delta_{\mathrm{meas}}(\lambda_i),
\qquad i=1,\dots,N,
\]
be given on a visible wavelength grid with \(N\ge 4\), and let
\[
\delta_{\mathrm{mod}}(\lambda_i;A,B,C)
\]
denote the best-fit modeled data induced by the first effective carrier-dispersion fit ansatz of Definition~\ref{def:first-effective-carrier-dispersion-fit-ansatz}. Let
\[
\Delta_{\delta}^{\mathrm{fit}}(\lambda_i)
=
\delta_{\mathrm{meas}}(\lambda_i)-\delta_{\mathrm{mod}}(\lambda_i;A,B,C)
\]
be the post-fit residual profile. Then the following first consistency reading is admissible:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=2em,label=(\roman*)]
  \item if the post-fit residual is uniformly small and preserves the ordinary wavelength ordering of the spectrum, then the reduced prism-readout sector is self-consistent at first approximation with the measured data;
  \item if the post-fit residual is small but carries a smooth systematic drift, then the reduced prism-readout sector remains viable at first approximation, but the effective carrier-dispersion profile requires refinement beyond the first three-parameter template;
  \item if the post-fit residual is not small and develops branch-like, split, or highly localized structure, then the first reduced optical sector is not yet sufficient by itself, and the discrepancy should be passed to the boundary/carrier/defect diagnostic layer rather than interpreted as evidence for a second foundational carrier.
\end{enumerate}
Thus overdetermined optical data may already be used to decide whether the first prism-readout model is merely coarse, needs refinement, or is visibly contaminated at the readout level.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
By Proposition~\ref{prop:first-three-parameter-spectral-calibration-principle}, the first ansatz already separates baseline, slope, and curvature contributions of the reduced carrier-side optical law. If \(N\ge 4\), then the data overdetermine the parameter triple \((A,B,C)\), so the remaining discrepancy cannot be absorbed merely by choosing those three parameters. If the resulting residual remains uniformly small while preserving the ordinary spectral ordering, then the same retained-carrier/prism sector already explains the data at first approximation. If the residual stays small but systematic and smooth, then the reduced sector is still viable, but the carrier-side refractive template is too coarse and requires higher-order refinement. If the residual instead shows splitting, localized spikes, or branch-like irregularity, then the residual spectral-diagnostic lemma applies: the discrepancy must first be read through boundary, carrier-profile, or defect/readout contamination channels inside the same reduced sector before postulating any stronger foundational change. Hence the stated three-way overdetermined consistency reading is admissible.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[First validation workflow for measured optical series]
\label{cor:first-validation-workflow-for-measured-optical-series}
Whenever a later argument in the present public v3.23.0 release line has at least four measured visible wavelength channels, it is sufficient to proceed in the following first validation workflow:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=2em,label=(\roman*)]
  \item fit \((A,B,C)\) on the reduced prism-readout sector;
  \item compute the overdetermined post-fit residual profile \(\Delta_{\delta}^{\mathrm{fit}}(\lambda_i)\);
  \item decide whether the reduced optical sector is already self-consistent, requires carrier-profile refinement, or shows boundary/defect/readout contamination;
  \item only after that decide whether a stronger optical law is genuinely needed.
\end{enumerate}
This prevents the first overdetermined mismatch from being overinterpreted too early as a failure of the retained carrier picture itself.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
This is the operational reformulation of Proposition~\ref{prop:first-overdetermined-spectral-consistency-principle}. The proposition already isolates the precise point at which overdetermined data can be used to validate or refine the reduced prism-readout sector before any stronger optical theory is invoked.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Status of the first effective-index reconstruction step in v3.23]
\label{rem:status-of-the-first-effective-index-reconstruction-step-in-v323}
The present public v3.23.0 release line still does \emph{not} claim a full global inversion of the whole crystal--shadow optical sector. What it now does support, however, is one first reconstruction step: once a reduced prism-readout sector has passed the first validation layer, measured prism-angle data may already be converted back into an effective refractive profile on the retained carrier surface.
\end{remark}

\begin{definition}[First reconstructed effective refractive profile]
\label{def:first-reconstructed-effective-refractive-profile}
Let a reduced prism-readout sector be given with fixed prism wedge angle
\[
A_{\mathrm{pr}}.
\]
Suppose that for each working wavelength channel \(\lambda\) a measured minimal-deviation angle
\[
\delta_{\min}^{\mathrm{meas}}(\lambda)
\]
is available. The \emph{first reconstructed effective refractive profile} is defined by
\[
n_{\mathrm{rec}}(\lambda)
:=
\frac{\sin\!\bigl((A_{\mathrm{pr}}+\delta_{\min}^{\mathrm{meas}}(\lambda))/2\bigr)}
     {\sin(A_{\mathrm{pr}}/2)}.
\]
This is the first reduced carrier-side inversion of prism-angle data back into an effective refractive law on the retained carrier surface.
\end{definition}

\begin{proposition}[First effective-index reconstruction principle from prism data]
\label{prop:first-effective-index-reconstruction-principle-from-prism-data}
Let a reduced prism-readout sector be given in the sense of Definition~\ref{def:reduced-prism-readout-sector}, and assume:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=2em,label=(\roman*)]
  \item the wedge geometry is fixed and the working optical data are taken in the minimal-deviation regime;
  \item the reduced prism-readout sector has already passed the first validation layer of Corollary~\ref{cor:first-validation-workflow-for-measured-optical-series} in the sense that its residual series is either already self-consistent at first approximation or requires only carrier-profile refinement;
  \item no stronger branch-splitting or second-carrier effect is being invoked.
\end{enumerate}
Then the measured minimal-deviation data determine a first reconstructed effective refractive profile
\[
n_{\mathrm{rec}}(\lambda)
\]
on the retained carrier surface. Moreover, the discrepancy
\[
\Delta_n^{\mathrm{rec}}(\lambda)
:=
n_{\mathrm{rec}}(\lambda)-n_{\mathrm{eff}}(\lambda)
\]
between reconstructed and fitted effective refractive profiles may be used as a second carrier-side diagnostic layer:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=2em,label=(\alph*)]
  \item if \(\Delta_n^{\mathrm{rec}}(\lambda)\) is uniformly small, then the fitted carrier-side ansatz already captures the first effective refractive behavior;
  \item if \(\Delta_n^{\mathrm{rec}}(\lambda)\) is smooth but systematic, then the retained carrier picture remains viable, but the dispersion template requires refinement;
  \item if \(\Delta_n^{\mathrm{rec}}(\lambda)\) develops irregular branch-like structure, then the discrepancy should be passed back to the defect/readout contamination layer rather than read as failure of the retained carrier itself.
\end{enumerate}
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
By Definition~\ref{def:first-reconstructed-effective-refractive-profile}, minimal-deviation prism data on a fixed wedge geometry already determine a reduced effective refractive profile \(n_{\mathrm{rec}}(\lambda)\). Assumption~(ii) says that the reduced prism-readout sector has already survived the first overdetermined validation layer, so the optical readout is not being discarded as an uncontrolled multi-foundational effect. Therefore the reconstructed profile may be read as a carrier-side optical summary on the same retained carrier surface. Comparing \(n_{\mathrm{rec}}(\lambda)\) to the fitted ansatz \(n_{\mathrm{eff}}(\lambda)\) produces a second diagnostic residual directly at the level of effective refractive law. If this discrepancy is small, the first carrier-side ansatz already captures the visible refractive behavior. If it is smooth but systematic, then the same retained carrier picture still works, but the template is too coarse. If it becomes irregular or branch-like, then the earlier residual-diagnostic layer applies and the discrepancy must first be read through defect/readout contamination channels. Hence the stated reconstruction principle is admissible.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[First inversion workflow from prism angles to carrier profile]
\label{cor:first-inversion-workflow-from-prism-angles-to-carrier-profile}
Whenever minimal-deviation prism-angle data are available in the present public v3.23.0 release line, it is sufficient to proceed in the following first inversion workflow:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=2em,label=(\roman*)]
  \item validate the reduced prism-readout sector by the overdetermined residual layer;
  \item reconstruct
  \[
  n_{\mathrm{rec}}(\lambda)
  \]
  from the measured minimal-deviation angles;
  \item compare \(n_{\mathrm{rec}}(\lambda)\) with the fitted effective carrier profile \(n_{\mathrm{eff}}(\lambda)\);
  \item classify the reconstruction discrepancy as already captured, refinement-worthy, or defect/readout contaminated.
\end{enumerate}
This gives a first direct route from measured prism data back to the retained carrier-side dispersion profile without invoking a full global optical inversion of the entire crystal--shadow architecture.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
This is the operational reformulation of Proposition~\ref{prop:first-effective-index-reconstruction-principle-from-prism-data}. The proposition already isolates the precise point at which measured prism-angle data can be pushed back to a first reconstructed refractive profile on the retained carrier surface.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Status of the first carrier-profile correction step in v3.23]
\label{rem:status-of-the-first-carrier-profile-correction-step-in-v323}
The present public v3.23.0 release line still does \emph{not} claim a final globally convergent refinement scheme for the full crystal--shadow optical law. What it now does support, however, is one first correction step for the reduced carrier-side dispersion template: the discrepancy between reconstructed and fitted effective refractive profiles may already be decomposed into baseline, slope, and curvature corrections of the same three-parameter carrier ansatz.
\end{remark}

\begin{definition}[First carrier-profile correction decomposition]
\label{def:first-carrier-profile-correction-decomposition}
Let
\[
n_{\mathrm{eff}}(\lambda)=A+\frac{B}{\lambda^2}+\frac{C}{\lambda^4}
\]
be the fitted effective carrier profile and let
\[
n_{\mathrm{rec}}(\lambda)
\]
be the reconstructed effective refractive profile from Definition~\ref{def:first-reconstructed-effective-refractive-profile}. The first carrier-profile correction decomposition writes the reconstruction discrepancy
\[
\Delta_n^{\mathrm{rec}}(\lambda)
=
n_{\mathrm{rec}}(\lambda)-n_{\mathrm{eff}}(\lambda)
\]
in the form
\[
\Delta_n^{\mathrm{rec}}(\lambda)
=
\Delta A+\frac{\Delta B}{\lambda^2}+\frac{\Delta C}{\lambda^4}
+
\mathfrak R_n(\lambda),
\]
where:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=2em,label=(\roman*)]
  \item \(\Delta A\) is the first carrier-baseline correction;
  \item \(\Delta B\) is the first dispersion-slope correction;
  \item \(\Delta C\) is the first curvature correction;
  \item \(\mathfrak R_n(\lambda)\) is the residual remainder not captured by the first carrier-side correction layer.
\end{enumerate}
\end{definition}

\begin{proposition}[First carrier-profile correction principle]
\label{prop:first-carrier-profile-correction-principle}
Let a reduced prism-readout sector be given on the retained carrier surface, and assume that:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=2em,label=(\roman*)]
  \item a fitted effective carrier profile \(n_{\mathrm{eff}}(\lambda)\) and a reconstructed profile \(n_{\mathrm{rec}}(\lambda)\) are both available;
  \item the reduced prism-readout sector has already passed the first validation layer in the sense that no second foundational carrier is being invoked;
  \item the reconstruction discrepancy \(\Delta_n^{\mathrm{rec}}(\lambda)\) is smooth enough across the working visible sector to admit a first carrier-side correction fit.
\end{enumerate}
Then the first carrier-profile correction decomposition of Definition~\ref{def:first-carrier-profile-correction-decomposition} is admissible, with the following reading:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=2em,label=(\alph*)]
  \item \(\Delta A\) shifts the coarse carrier baseline level;
  \item \(\Delta B\) shifts the dominant red-to-blue dispersion slope;
  \item \(\Delta C\) shifts the first higher-order curvature of the visible spacing;
  \item the remainder \(\mathfrak R_n(\lambda)\) measures whatever is still not captured by the first carrier-side refinement and should therefore be passed back to the residual diagnostic layer.
\end{enumerate}
In particular, the carrier-side ansatz may already be updated once by
\[
A\mapsto A+\Delta A,\qquad
B\mapsto B+\Delta B,\qquad
C\mapsto C+\Delta C
\]
before any stronger global optical law is introduced.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
By Proposition~\ref{prop:first-effective-index-reconstruction-principle-from-prism-data}, the reconstructed effective refractive profile \(n_{\mathrm{rec}}(\lambda)\) is already readable as a carrier-side optical summary whenever the reduced prism-readout sector has survived the first validation layer. The fitted profile \(n_{\mathrm{eff}}(\lambda)\) and the reconstructed profile \(n_{\mathrm{rec}}(\lambda)\) therefore live on the same retained carrier picture. Since the original effective carrier law was organized by the basis functions \(1,\lambda^{-2},\lambda^{-4}\), the first smooth discrepancy between reconstructed and fitted profiles may be decomposed against the same basis before introducing any stronger law. The coefficients of that decomposition are exactly the first baseline, slope, and curvature corrections, while any uncaptured remainder must still be handled by the residual diagnostic layer. Hence the stated first correction principle is admissible.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[First refinement workflow for the effective carrier law]
\label{cor:first-refinement-workflow-for-the-effective-carrier-law}
Whenever reconstructed and fitted effective refractive profiles are both available in the present public v3.23.0 release line, it is sufficient to proceed in the following first refinement workflow:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=2em,label=(\roman*)]
  \item form the reconstruction discrepancy \(\Delta_n^{\mathrm{rec}}(\lambda)\);
  \item fit the first carrier-side correction triple \((\Delta A,\Delta B,\Delta C)\);
  \item update the effective carrier law by
  \[
  (A,B,C)\mapsto(A+\Delta A,B+\Delta B,C+\Delta C);
  \]
  \item pass the uncaptured remainder \(\mathfrak R_n(\lambda)\) back to the residual diagnostic layer.
\end{enumerate}
This gives the first iterative correction step for the reduced optical sector without postulating a full global inversion theory of the whole crystal--shadow architecture.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
This is the operational reformulation of Proposition~\ref{prop:first-carrier-profile-correction-principle}. The proposition already isolates the precise point at which reconstructed-versus-fitted refractive discrepancies can be turned into the first explicit carrier-side update step.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Status of the first reduced spectral-stability step in v3.23]
\label{rem:status-of-the-first-reduced-spectral-stability-step-in-v323}
The present public v3.23.0 release line still does \emph{not} claim a final convergence theory for arbitrary iterative optical refinements. What it now does support, however, is one first reduced stability rule: after one carrier-side correction step, the reduced prism-readout sector may already be judged stable enough for first-order spectral use if the updated residual remains small and preserves the ordinary wavelength ordering.
\end{remark}

\begin{proposition}[First reduced spectral-stability principle]
\label{prop:first-reduced-spectral-stability-principle}
Let
\[
n_{\mathrm{eff}}^{(1)}(\lambda)
=
(A+\Delta A)+\frac{B+\Delta B}{\lambda^2}+\frac{C+\Delta C}{\lambda^4}
\]
be the once-refined effective carrier law produced by the first refinement workflow of Corollary~\ref{cor:first-refinement-workflow-for-the-effective-carrier-law}. Let
\[
\delta_{\mathrm{mod}}^{(1)}(\lambda_i)
\]
denote the corresponding updated modeled prism-output data, and let
\[
\Delta_{\delta}^{(1)}(\lambda_i)
:=
\delta_{\mathrm{meas}}(\lambda_i)-\delta_{\mathrm{mod}}^{(1)}(\lambda_i)
\]
be the updated post-refinement residual series. Assume that:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=2em,label=(\roman*)]
  \item the reduced prism-readout sector continues to satisfy the no-second-carrier / defect-subordination assumptions of the earlier optical layer;
  \item the updated residual \(\Delta_{\delta}^{(1)}(\lambda_i)\) is uniformly smaller than the pre-refinement residual in the working visible sector;
  \item the ordinary wavelength ordering of the spectrum is preserved after refinement.
\end{enumerate}
Then the once-refined reduced prism-readout sector is already spectrally stable at first order: it may be used as a stable first-order carrier-side optical model for current spectral approximation purposes without yet invoking a stronger global optical law of the full crystal--shadow architecture.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
By Corollary~\ref{cor:first-refinement-workflow-for-the-effective-carrier-law}, the first carrier-side correction step updates the effective refractive template using baseline, slope, and curvature corrections extracted from reconstructed-versus-fitted refractive discrepancies. If assumption~(i) holds, then the refinement remains inside the same retained carrier picture and does not open a competing optical foundation. If assumption~(ii) holds, the updated model explains the measured optical data strictly better than the previous one at the level of the working residual. If assumption~(iii) holds, the reduced prism-readout sector still reproduces the ordinary spectral ordering that defines the intended optical regime. Hence the updated model is not merely numerically altered but improved while staying inside the same reduced optical sector. This is exactly the first reduced stability claim.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[First stopping rule for the reduced prism-readout fit loop]
\label{cor:first-stopping-rule-for-the-reduced-prism-readout-fit-loop}
Whenever a later argument in the present public v3.23.0 release line performs one or more carrier-side correction steps inside the reduced prism-readout sector, it is sufficient to stop the first refinement loop once:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=2em,label=(\roman*)]
  \item the residual is no longer structurally improving in a meaningful way,
  \item the ordinary wavelength ordering is preserved,
  \item and no new branch-like or defect-type irregularity appears.
\end{enumerate}
At that point the resulting reduced optical law may be used as the active first-order spectral model, and any remaining discrepancy should be passed to the residual diagnostic layer or deferred to a stronger later optical theory.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
This is the operational reformulation of Proposition~\ref{prop:first-reduced-spectral-stability-principle}. The proposition already isolates the precise point at which the refined prism-readout sector becomes stable enough for first-order spectral use without forcing a stronger global optical model.
\end{proof}


\begin{remark}[Status of the first bundled optical approximation package in v3.23]
\label{rem:status-of-the-first-bundled-optical-approximation-package-in-v323}
The present public v3.23.0 release line still does \emph{not} claim a full optical theory of the complete crystal--shadow architecture. What it now does support, however, is one first bundled optical approximation package on the retained carrier surface: reduced prism readout, residual diagnostics, carrier-side fit, calibration, validation, inversion, refinement, and reduced stability may now be cited together as one coherent first-order optical layer.
\end{remark}

\begin{proposition}[First bundled optical approximation package]
\label{prop:first-bundled-optical-approximation-package}
On the retained carrier surface of the present public v3.23.0 release line, the following first-order optical ingredients are now available together:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=2em,label=(\roman*)]
  \item by Lemma~\ref{lem:first-prism-readout-lemma-on-the-retained-carrier-surface}, one reduced prism-readout sector with ordinary wavelength ordering;
  \item by Lemma~\ref{lem:first-residual-spectral-diagnostic-lemma}, one structured residual diagnostic layer for measured-versus-modeled prism data;
  \item by Proposition~\ref{prop:first-parametric-spectral-fit-principle}, one first carrier-side three-parameter dispersion fit ansatz;
  \item by Proposition~\ref{prop:first-three-parameter-spectral-calibration-principle}, one first calibration rule for the parameter triple \((A,B,C)\);
  \item by Proposition~\ref{prop:first-overdetermined-spectral-consistency-principle}, one first validation rule for overdetermined optical series;
  \item by Proposition~\ref{prop:first-effective-index-reconstruction-principle-from-prism-data}, one first inversion route from prism angles back to an effective refractive profile;
  \item by Proposition~\ref{prop:first-carrier-profile-correction-principle}, one first explicit correction step for the effective carrier law;
  \item by Proposition~\ref{prop:first-reduced-spectral-stability-principle}, one first reduced stability and stopping rule for the fit/refinement loop.
\end{enumerate}
Therefore the current line already contains one bundled first-order optical approximation layer on the retained carrier surface.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Each clause is exactly one optical step already established in the present line. The only new point here is bundling: these steps no longer appear as unrelated local add-ons, but as one coherent workflow on the same retained carrier picture. Clause (i) isolates the reduced optical sector. Clauses (ii)--(v) organize data comparison, parameter fitting, calibration, and validation. Clauses (vi)--(vii) push the fitted optical law back to a reconstructed carrier profile and allow one explicit update step. Clause (viii) supplies the first reduced stability criterion. Taken together, these clauses form one coherent first-order optical approximation package.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Bundled use rule for the first optical approximation package]
\label{cor:bundled-use-rule-for-the-first-optical-approximation-package}
Whenever a later argument in the present public v3.23.0 release line stays inside the reduced retained-carrier optical sector and needs only first-order optical reasoning, it is sufficient to cite Proposition~\ref{prop:first-bundled-optical-approximation-package} and work with the bundled optical approximation package rather than reopening each individual optical step separately. A finer reopening is required only when the argument depends on a stronger global optical theory, a non-reduced anisotropic branch, or a second-order refinement beyond the present first loop.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
This is the operational reformulation of Proposition~\ref{prop:first-bundled-optical-approximation-package}. The proposition already isolates the precise point at which the current optical workflow can be used as one common first-order layer on the retained carrier surface.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Status of the first data-anchored optical comparison step in v3.24]
\label{rem:status-of-the-first-data-anchored-optical-comparison-step-in-v324}
The present v3.24.0 working line still does \emph{not} claim a final material-identification theorem for the complete crystal--shadow architecture. What it now does support, however, is one first data-anchored comparison step: a reduced retained-carrier optical series may already be compared against an external reference optical series and read as a first material-style fingerprint on the same carrier-side approximation layer.
\end{remark}

\begin{definition}[Reference-comparison optical signature]
\label{def:reference-comparison-optical-signature}
Let
\[
S_{\mathrm{mod}}(\lambda_i)
\]
denote any reduced retained-carrier optical series produced by the bundled optical approximation package, for example an angle series \(\delta_{\mathrm{mod}}(\lambda_i)\), a reconstructed refractive series \(n_{\mathrm{rec}}(\lambda_i)\), or a refined carrier profile \(n_{\mathrm{eff}}^{(1)}(\lambda_i)\). Let
\[
S_{\mathrm{ref}}(\lambda_i)
\]
denote an external reference optical series measured on the same wavelength grid. The corresponding \emph{reference-comparison optical signature} is the discrepancy profile
\[
\Sigma_{\mathrm{opt}}(\lambda_i)
:=
S_{\mathrm{ref}}(\lambda_i)-S_{\mathrm{mod}}(\lambda_i).
\]
\end{definition}

\begin{proposition}[First data-anchored optical comparison principle]
\label{prop:first-data-anchored-optical-comparison-principle}
Let a reduced retained-carrier optical series \(S_{\mathrm{mod}}(\lambda_i)\) be given by the bundled optical approximation package of Proposition~\ref{prop:first-bundled-optical-approximation-package}, and let \(S_{\mathrm{ref}}(\lambda_i)\) be an external reference optical series on the same wavelength grid. Assume that:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=2em,label=(\roman*)]
  \item the internal reduced optical sector has already been validated to first order on its own terms;
  \item the reference series is used only as an external comparison anchor and not as a second foundational carrier;
  \item the comparison is made at the level of the same optical observable, e.g. angle-to-angle or refractive-profile-to-refractive-profile.
\end{enumerate}
Then the discrepancy profile
\[
\Sigma_{\mathrm{opt}}(\lambda_i)
\]
may already be read as a first material-style optical signature with the following interpretation:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=2em,label=(\alph*)]
  \item if \(\Sigma_{\mathrm{opt}}(\lambda_i)\) is uniformly small, then the reduced retained-carrier optical sector is first-order compatible with the chosen reference family;
  \item if \(\Sigma_{\mathrm{opt}}(\lambda_i)\) is smooth and systematic, then the same retained-carrier optical family remains viable but sits in a shifted or refined material-style subclass relative to the chosen reference;
  \item if \(\Sigma_{\mathrm{opt}}(\lambda_i)\) is irregular, branch-like, or strongly localized, then the discrepancy should first be passed back to the boundary/carrier/defect diagnostic layer rather than read as direct evidence of reference-family equivalence.
\end{enumerate}
Thus external data comparison may already be used to produce a first optical fingerprint without abandoning the retained-carrier picture.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
By Proposition~\ref{prop:first-bundled-optical-approximation-package}, the current line already supplies a coherent first-order optical package on the retained carrier surface. Assumption~(i) says that the internal reduced optical sector has already survived its own validation layer, so the comparison does not begin from an uncontrolled model. Assumption~(ii) ensures that the external reference series functions only as a comparison anchor, not as a second carrier. Assumption~(iii) ensures that the discrepancy profile compares like with like. Therefore the remaining discrepancy \(\Sigma_{\mathrm{opt}}(\lambda_i)\) can be read as an optical signature of how the retained-carrier approximation sits relative to the chosen reference family. If the discrepancy is uniformly small, compatibility with that family is the first admissible reading. If the discrepancy is smooth and systematic, then the same family remains viable but requires shifted/refined parameter placement. If the discrepancy is irregular, the earlier residual/boundary/defect diagnostics must be reopened before any stronger material identification claim is made. Hence the stated comparison principle is admissible.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[First material-signature workflow for optical reference data]
\label{cor:first-material-signature-workflow-for-optical-reference-data}
Whenever external optical reference data are available in the present v3.24.0 working line, it is sufficient to proceed in the following first workflow:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=2em,label=(\roman*)]
  \item build or validate the reduced retained-carrier optical series \(S_{\mathrm{mod}}(\lambda_i)\);
  \item compare it against a same-observable reference series \(S_{\mathrm{ref}}(\lambda_i)\);
  \item form the optical signature profile \(\Sigma_{\mathrm{opt}}(\lambda_i)\);
  \item classify the result as first-order compatible, smoothly shifted/refined, or diagnostically irregular.
\end{enumerate}
This gives the first data-anchored optical comparison layer of the project without claiming a final material-identification theorem.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
This is the operational reformulation of Proposition~\ref{prop:first-data-anchored-optical-comparison-principle}. The proposition already isolates the precise point at which reference comparison becomes a controlled first optical fingerprinting step.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Status of the first reference-family comparison framework in v3.24]
\label{rem:status-of-the-first-reference-family-comparison-framework-in-v324}
The present v3.24.0 working line still does \emph{not} claim a final unique material identification theorem for the full crystal--shadow architecture. What it now does support, however, is one first reference-family comparison framework: candidate optical reference families may already be ranked against the retained-carrier optical signature by the size and regularity of the comparison discrepancy.
\end{remark}

\begin{definition}[Reference-family comparison score]
\label{def:reference-family-comparison-score}
Let
\[
S_{\mathrm{mod}}(\lambda_i)
\]
be a reduced retained-carrier optical series and let
\[
\{S_{\mathrm{ref}}^{(\alpha)}(\lambda_i)\}_{\alpha\in\mathcal A}
\]
be a finite family of candidate reference optical series on the same wavelength grid. For each candidate family label \(\alpha\), define the comparison discrepancy
\[
\Sigma_{\mathrm{opt}}^{(\alpha)}(\lambda_i)
:=
S_{\mathrm{ref}}^{(\alpha)}(\lambda_i)-S_{\mathrm{mod}}(\lambda_i).
\]
A \emph{reference-family comparison score} is any first-order scalar summary
\[
\mathfrak S(\alpha)
\]
that increases when the discrepancy becomes larger or more irregular and decreases when the discrepancy is smaller and more regular across the working wavelength grid.
\end{definition}

\begin{proposition}[First reference-family ranking principle]
\label{prop:first-reference-family-ranking-principle}
Let a reduced retained-carrier optical series \(S_{\mathrm{mod}}(\lambda_i)\) be given together with a finite candidate family of reference optical series
\[
\{S_{\mathrm{ref}}^{(\alpha)}(\lambda_i)\}_{\alpha\in\mathcal A}.
\]
Assume that:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=2em,label=(\roman*)]
  \item each reference family is compared on the same wavelength grid and at the same observable level as \(S_{\mathrm{mod}}(\lambda_i)\);
  \item the reduced retained-carrier optical sector has already been validated internally at first order;
  \item the comparison score \(\mathfrak S(\alpha)\) is chosen so that both size and irregularity of the discrepancy profile penalize the score.
\end{enumerate}
Then the candidate families may already be ranked by \(\mathfrak S(\alpha)\) with the following first reading:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=2em,label=(\alph*)]
  \item families with the smallest scores are first-order optical comparison candidates for the present retained-carrier sector;
  \item families with slightly larger but still smooth scores define a shifted or refined comparison shell around the best candidates;
  \item families with large or highly irregular scores are not first-order comparison candidates at the present retained-carrier optical level.
\end{enumerate}
Thus the optical signature may already be used to construct a first ranked shortlist of material-style comparison families without claiming unique identification.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
By Proposition~\ref{prop:first-data-anchored-optical-comparison-principle}, a discrepancy profile between the retained-carrier optical series and a given reference series may already be read as a first material-style optical signature. If this is done for each candidate family on the same wavelength grid and same observable level, then each family carries its own discrepancy profile \(\Sigma_{\mathrm{opt}}^{(\alpha)}(\lambda_i)\). A comparison score that penalizes both large size and strong irregularity exactly preserves the first-order diagnostic reading of the previous comparison layer: smaller and smoother discrepancy indicates closer first-order compatibility, while larger or more irregular discrepancy indicates poorer compatibility or diagnostic mismatch. Therefore ordering the candidates by \(\mathfrak S(\alpha)\) yields a first admissible ranking and hence a first shortlist of comparison families.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[First shortlist workflow for candidate optical families]
\label{cor:first-shortlist-workflow-for-candidate-optical-families}
Whenever multiple external reference families are available in the present v3.24.0 working line, it is sufficient to proceed in the following first shortlist workflow:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=2em,label=(\roman*)]
  \item compute the discrepancy profile \(\Sigma_{\mathrm{opt}}^{(\alpha)}(\lambda_i)\) for each candidate family;
  \item evaluate a first comparison score \(\mathfrak S(\alpha)\) for each candidate;
  \item rank the candidates from smallest to largest score;
  \item treat the lowest-score families as the active first-order comparison shortlist and pass only those to any stronger later material-style or structural diagnostic layer.
\end{enumerate}
This gives the first concrete comparison framework for reference materials on the retained-carrier optical side without postulating unique optical identification.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
This is the operational reformulation of Proposition~\ref{prop:first-reference-family-ranking-principle}. The proposition already isolates the precise point at which multiple reference families may be turned into a ranked shortlist on the basis of first-order optical signature comparison.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Status of the first structural back-reading step from optical shortlists in v3.24]
\label{rem:status-of-the-first-structural-back-reading-step-from-optical-shortlists-in-v324}
The present v3.24.0 working line still does \emph{not} claim a final theorem identifying structural origin uniquely from optical comparison data alone. What it now does support, however, is one first structural back-reading step: the pattern of best optical comparison families may already be read as a first indication of whether the active discrepancy is predominantly boundary-driven, carrier-profile-driven, or defect/readout-driven.
\end{remark}

\begin{definition}[Optical shortlist back-reading pattern]
\label{def:optical-shortlist-back-reading-pattern}
Let
\[
\mathcal A_{\mathrm{short}}
\subseteq
\mathcal A
\]
be the shortlist of best optical comparison families obtained from Corollary~\ref{cor:first-shortlist-workflow-for-candidate-optical-families}. The corresponding \emph{optical shortlist back-reading pattern} is the qualitative distribution of the shortlisted families according to whether their low-score similarity is governed primarily by:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=2em,label=(\roman*)]
  \item boundary/wedge alignment behavior;
  \item carrier-dispersion profile behavior;
  \item defect/readout irregularity behavior.
\end{enumerate}
\end{definition}

\begin{proposition}[First structural back-reading principle from optical shortlists]
\label{prop:first-structural-back-reading-principle-from-optical-shortlists}
Let a reduced retained-carrier optical series be compared against a finite candidate family of reference optical series, and let
\[
\mathcal A_{\mathrm{short}}
\]
be the resulting shortlist of best first-order comparison candidates. Assume that:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=2em,label=(\roman*)]
  \item the shortlisted candidates have been obtained on a common wavelength grid and at the same observable level;
  \item the reduced retained-carrier optical sector has already passed its internal first-order validation;
  \item the shortlist is rich enough to distinguish whether low-score similarity is driven mainly by boundary placement, by carrier-dispersion shape, or by defect/readout regularity.
\end{enumerate}
Then the shortlist may already be read back structurally in the following first sense:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=2em,label=(\alph*)]
  \item if the shortlist is dominated by families that agree mainly through global offset and wedge-placement behavior, then the active comparison should first be read as boundary-dominated;
  \item if the shortlist is dominated by families that agree mainly through smooth wavelength-ordering shape and dispersion curvature, then the active comparison should first be read as carrier-profile-dominated;
  \item if the shortlist is unstable, mixed, or only attainable through families carrying irregular local features, then the active comparison should first be read as defect/readout-dominated.
\end{enumerate}
Thus a first structural back-reading is already admissible from the pattern of best optical comparison families, without claiming unique structural identification.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
By Proposition~\ref{prop:first-reference-family-ranking-principle}, the optical comparison layer already orders candidate families by size and regularity of their discrepancy against the reduced retained-carrier optical series. The only new point here is to read the geometry of that shortlist rather than only its ranking. If the low-score families agree mainly through global offset and wedge placement, then the previous residual diagnostic layer already indicates a boundary-style source of mismatch. If the low-score families agree mainly through smooth dispersive shape and curvature, then the same retained-carrier optical series is being matched primarily at the level of carrier-dispersion profile, so a carrier-profile reading is first admissible. If, however, the shortlist remains unstable or only becomes competitive through irregular local features, then the comparison is being controlled by the same kind of branch-like or localized irregularity that the earlier diagnostic layer associates first with defect/readout contamination. Hence the stated first structural back-reading is admissible.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[First workflow from optical shortlist to structural diagnostic hint]
\label{cor:first-workflow-from-optical-shortlist-to-structural-diagnostic-hint}
Whenever a later argument in the present v3.24.0 working line has already produced a shortlist of best optical comparison families, it is sufficient to proceed in the following first structural back-reading workflow:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=2em,label=(\roman*)]
  \item inspect whether the shortlist is primarily boundary-like, carrier-shape-like, or irregular/defect-like;
  \item assign the active comparison a first structural diagnostic hint of boundary, carrier, or defect/readout dominance;
  \item use that hint to decide which internal diagnostic layer should be reopened first if stronger refinement is needed.
\end{enumerate}
This gives a first controlled route from optical comparison shortlists back to structural diagnostics without claiming a final unique material theorem.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
This is the operational reformulation of Proposition~\ref{prop:first-structural-back-reading-principle-from-optical-shortlists}. The proposition already isolates the precise point at which an optical shortlist can be turned into a first structural diagnostic hint.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Status of the first diagnostic reopening-priority step in v3.24]
\label{rem:status-of-the-first-diagnostic-reopening-priority-step-in-v324}
The present v3.24.0 working line still does \emph{not} claim a final convergent refinement algorithm for every optical mismatch pattern. What it now does support, however, is one first reopening-priority rule: once an optical shortlist has been read back structurally, the order in which internal diagnostic layers should be reopened may already be chosen in a controlled way.
\end{remark}

\begin{definition}[Structural diagnostic reopening priority]
\label{def:structural-diagnostic-reopening-priority}
Let a first structural diagnostic hint have been assigned from Corollary~\ref{cor:first-workflow-from-optical-shortlist-to-structural-diagnostic-hint}. The corresponding \emph{structural diagnostic reopening priority} is the ordered choice of the internal diagnostic layers to be reopened first among the three first-order sectors:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=2em,label=(\roman*)]
  \item the boundary/wedge alignment layer;
  \item the carrier-profile and dispersion-shape layer;
  \item the defect/readout irregularity layer.
\end{enumerate}
A reopening priority is called \emph{pure} if one of these layers is selected strictly first, and \emph{mixed} if two layers must be reopened together before a stronger conclusion is drawn.
\end{definition}

\begin{proposition}[First diagnostic reopening-priority principle from optical back-reading]
\label{prop:first-diagnostic-reopening-priority-principle-from-optical-back-reading}
Assume that a reduced retained-carrier optical series has already produced:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=2em,label=(\roman*)]
  \item a validated first-order optical comparison layer;
  \item a ranked shortlist of best comparison families;
  \item a first structural diagnostic hint of boundary, carrier, or defect/readout dominance.
\end{enumerate}
Then the internal diagnostic reopening may already be prioritized in the following first sense:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=2em,label=(\alph*)]
  \item if the hint is boundary-dominated, reopen the boundary/wedge alignment layer first and postpone finer defect/readout interpretation until that boundary recalibration has been checked;
  \item if the hint is carrier-profile-dominated, reopen the carrier-dispersion layer first and postpone finer defect/readout interpretation until the smooth carrier profile has been refit or rejected;
  \item if the hint is defect/readout-dominated, reopen the defect/readout irregularity layer first, but only after confirming that the mismatch cannot already be removed by a simple boundary or carrier-side adjustment inside the validated first-order optical sector;
  \item if the hint is genuinely mixed between boundary and carrier behavior, reopen those two smooth first-order layers together before escalating to a stronger structural claim.
\end{enumerate}
Thus the optical back-reading layer already determines a first controlled order in which structural diagnostics should be refined, without claiming final convergence or unique inverse reconstruction.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Corollary~\ref{cor:first-workflow-from-optical-shortlist-to-structural-diagnostic-hint} already turns the optical shortlist into a first structural hint. The only additional point is to convert that hint into an ordered reopening rule. If the shortlist is boundary-like, then the low-score compatibility is being governed primarily by offset or wedge-placement behavior, so the boundary layer is the first place where refinement can pay off. If the shortlist is carrier-shape-like, then the decisive structure lies in smooth wavelength-ordering and curvature, so the carrier-profile layer is the first place where refinement can pay off. If the shortlist is irregular or defect-like, then defect/readout diagnostics become first relevant, but only after the smoother boundary and carrier explanations have been checked away, because the earlier optical approximation package already treats those smooth sectors as the default low-order explanation class. Finally, if the shortlist is genuinely mixed between boundary and carrier behavior, then reopening only one of those two smooth layers would artificially force the comparison into a one-sided reading. Hence the stated first reopening-priority rule is admissible.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[First refinement workflow after optical back-reading]
\label{cor:first-refinement-workflow-after-optical-back-reading}
Whenever a later argument in the present v3.24.0 working line has already assigned a first structural diagnostic hint from an optical shortlist, it is sufficient to proceed in the following first refinement workflow:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=2em,label=(\roman*)]
  \item choose the reopening priority from Definition~\ref{def:structural-diagnostic-reopening-priority};
  \item reopen the corresponding smooth boundary or carrier layer first whenever the hint is not yet defect-dominated;
  \item reopen the defect/readout layer first only when irregularity remains after the smooth first-order explanations have been checked or when the shortlist is already genuinely irregular from the start;
  \item return to the optical residual layer and test whether the refined diagnosis improves the shortlist structure.
\end{enumerate}
This gives a first controlled loop from optical comparison to structural reopening and back to optical residual testing, without postulating a final globally convergent inversion scheme.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
This is the operational reformulation of Proposition~\ref{prop:first-diagnostic-reopening-priority-principle-from-optical-back-reading}. The proposition already isolates the precise point at which a structural hint can be converted into an ordered refinement loop.
\end{proof}















\begin{remark}[Status of the first bombe-guided refinement step in v3.24]
\label{rem:status-of-the-first-bombe-guided-refinement-step-in-v324}
The present v3.24.0 working line still does \emph{not} claim a global inverse solver that reconstructs the full internal architecture from optical data alone. What it now does support, however, is one first local bombe-guided refinement step: once an optical shortlist has been read back into a reopening priority, finite menus of reopening candidates may be filtered by contradiction-sensitive elimination instead of being explored blindly.
\end{remark}

\begin{definition}[Structural bombe on a reopening menu]
\label{def:structural-bombe-on-a-reopening-menu}
Assume that an optical shortlist has already produced a first structural diagnostic hint and a reopening priority as in Definition~\ref{def:structural-diagnostic-reopening-priority}. A \emph{structural bombe on a reopening menu} is a finite contradiction-sensitive elimination procedure applied to a finite candidate menu
\[
\mathcal M_0=\{\mu_1,\dots,\mu_N\},
\]
of admissible local reopening settings compatible with that priority, where each candidate $\mu_j$ specifies one local choice among boundary, carrier, defect/readout, or mixed refinements together with the corresponding low-order fit parameters allowed at the present stage.

The bombe acts on $\mathcal M_0$ by testing each candidate against the following first local filters:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=2em,label=(\roman*)]
  \item compatibility with the optical back-reading class that generated the menu;
  \item compatibility with the already validated closure/transport constraints of the present first-order optical sector;
  \item non-worsening, or first controlled improvement, of the optical residual pattern after the corresponding reopening step;
  \item absence of an immediate contradiction that forces the candidate outside the admissible low-order reading.
\end{enumerate}
A candidate that fails one of these filters is \emph{eliminated}; a candidate that passes all current filters is \emph{retained} for the next refinement stage.
\end{definition}

\begin{proposition}[First structural bombe elimination principle on reopening menus]
\label{prop:first-structural-bombe-elimination-principle-on-reopening-menus}
Assume that:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=2em,label=(\roman*)]
  \item a first optical shortlist and a first reopening priority have already been fixed;
  \item the corresponding reopening menu $\mathcal M_0$ is finite;
  \item the active filter family in Definition~\ref{def:structural-bombe-on-a-reopening-menu} is eliminative in the sense that failure of one filter already suffices to rule out the candidate at the present stage.
\end{enumerate}
Then the corresponding structural bombe may eliminate inadmissible reopening candidates without first reconstructing the full internal structure. In particular, the bombe may already reduce the menu to a smaller surviving set of reopening candidates whose residual behavior is compatible with the current optical back-reading class.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
The point is purely structural. By construction, the reopening menu is not the full hidden state space but only the finite local menu compatible with the already established optical back-reading and reopening priority. Hence the task is not global reconstruction but local elimination. If a candidate violates the back-reading class, it cannot be the correct local reopening at the present stage. If it violates validated closure/transport constraints, it is incompatible with the already fixed infrastructure. If it worsens the optical residual pattern in a way not allowed by the current first-order reading, then it fails as a refinement of the very discrepancy it was meant to address. Finally, if it immediately forces the argument outside the admissible low-order regime, then it is not a valid current-stage reopening candidate. Therefore any candidate failing one of the filters may be removed without waiting for a final inverse theorem. What remains is a strictly smaller surviving menu of locally admissible candidates.
\end{proof}

\begin{definition}[Nested structural bombe]
\label{def:nested-structural-bombe}
A \emph{nested structural bombe} is an iterated family of structural bombes arranged along a finite reopening tree
\[
\mathcal T=\bigl(\mathcal M^{(0)},\mathcal M^{(1)},\dots,\mathcal M^{(d)}\bigr),
\]
where:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=2em,label=(\roman*)]
  \item $\mathcal M^{(0)}$ is the first reopening menu produced from the optical back-reading stage;
  \item each surviving candidate at depth $k$ may open a new local submenu $\mathcal M^{(k+1)}$ refining the next structural layer beneath it;
  \item elimination at depth $k+1$ is propagated back upward by removing the parent candidate whenever all of its children are eliminated;
  \item survival at depth $k+1$ is propagated back upward by retaining the parent candidate as an unresolved but still admissible branch.
\end{enumerate}
Thus a nested structural bombe implements a controlled local backtracking across several reopening depths rather than a single flat elimination pass.
\end{definition}

\begin{proposition}[Nested bombe backtracking principle]
\label{prop:nested-bombe-backtracking-principle}
Assume that a first reopening menu has been constructed from optical back-reading and that deeper structural layers can be opened only through finite local submenus attached to surviving parent candidates. Then a nested structural bombe may be run depth by depth so that:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=2em,label=(\alph*)]
  \item contradictions discovered in a deeper submenu eliminate the corresponding parent candidate whenever no admissible child survives;
  \item a parent candidate survives provisionally as long as at least one admissible child branch remains open;
  \item the resulting backtracking tree never needs to explore a branch that has already been eliminated at a lower depth;
  \item mixed boundary/carrier/defect cases may therefore be refined in stages from the smooth outer layer toward deeper localized readout structure.
\end{enumerate}
Hence the bombe logic may be nested: first solve or eliminate the coarse reopening menu, then descend one layer further only along the branches that remain structurally alive.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
This is the natural tree version of Proposition~\ref{prop:first-structural-bombe-elimination-principle-on-reopening-menus}. At depth zero one has only the coarse reopening menu determined by optical back-reading. Any surviving parent candidate represents a still-admissible coarse interpretation. If that interpretation is refined one layer deeper, the child submenu records the next structural decisions compatible with the parent. When all such children fail, the parent can no longer represent an admissible reopening path and must be removed. When at least one child survives, the parent remains provisionally open because the deeper contradiction test has not closed the whole branch. Since every eliminated child closes only its own local branch, the procedure is genuine backtracking rather than uncontrolled restart: one returns upward only to remove or retain the corresponding parent. Therefore the elimination can proceed outward-to-inward and inward-to-outward in a disciplined layered way.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Layered bombe workflow from optical back-reading]
\label{cor:layered-bombe-workflow-from-optical-back-reading}
Whenever a later argument in the present v3.24.0 working line has already produced an optical shortlist and a reopening priority, it is sufficient to proceed in the following bombe-guided workflow:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=2em,label=(\roman*)]
  \item build the first reopening menu compatible with the optical back-reading class;
  \item run a structural bombe on that menu and eliminate immediately contradictory coarse candidates;
  \item for each surviving candidate, open only the next finite local submenu needed for deeper refinement;
  \item propagate eliminations upward whenever a submenu dies completely;
  \item return to the optical residual layer after each surviving depth and test whether the shortlist stabilizes, improves, or changes class.
\end{enumerate}
This gives a first controlled nested backtracking logic from optical comparison through layered structural reopening and back to the residual surface, without postulating a globally complete solver.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Corollary~\ref{cor:first-refinement-workflow-after-optical-back-reading} already gives the first loop from optical shortlist to reopening and back to the residual layer. Definition~\ref{def:structural-bombe-on-a-reopening-menu} turns that loop into a contradiction-sensitive elimination rule on each local menu, while Definition~\ref{def:nested-structural-bombe} adds the layered backtracking logic needed when one menu alone does not settle the local picture. Proposition~\ref{prop:nested-bombe-backtracking-principle} then shows that the refinement may descend one layer further only along surviving branches and may propagate elimination upward whenever a deeper submenu collapses completely. This is exactly the stated layered bombe workflow.
\end{proof}


\begin{remark}[Status of the first bombe-applied optical test case in v3.24]
\label{rem:status-of-the-first-bombe-applied-optical-test-case-in-v324}
The present v3.24.0 working line still does \emph{not} claim that every optical shortlist can already be resolved uniquely by bombe logic alone. What it now does support, however, is one first genuinely applied test case: the bombe framework can already be run on the first smooth mixed shortlist case and can thereby reduce a locally ambiguous reopening picture to a smaller and more structured surviving branch set.
\end{remark}

\begin{definition}[First smooth mixed shortlist case]
\label{def:first-smooth-mixed-shortlist-case}
A reduced retained-carrier optical comparison is said to be in the \emph{first smooth mixed shortlist case} if the following hold simultaneously:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=2em,label=(\roman*)]
  \item the lowest comparison scores belong to a finite optical shortlist whose best families are smooth and regular rather than spike-dominated or branch-dominated;
  \item the back-reading of Corollary~\ref{cor:first-workflow-from-optical-shortlist-to-structural-diagnostic-hint} is mixed between boundary-like and carrier-shape-like behavior;
  \item no dominant localized irregularity forces defect/readout reopening to the front of the diagnostic order;
  \item the reopening priority of Definition~\ref{def:structural-diagnostic-reopening-priority} is therefore mixed between boundary and carrier-profile refinement.
\end{enumerate}
In that case the first reopening menu may be written schematically as
\[
\mathcal M_0^{\mathrm{mix}}=\{\mu_{\mathrm B},\mu_{\mathrm C},\mu_{\mathrm{BC}},\mu_{\mathrm D}\},
\]
where \(\mu_{\mathrm B}\) denotes pure boundary recalibration, \(\mu_{\mathrm C}\) pure carrier-profile refinement, \(\mu_{\mathrm{BC}}\) a mixed boundary/carrier reopening, and \(\mu_{\mathrm D}\) an early defect/readout reopening candidate.
\end{definition}

\begin{proposition}[First bombe reduction in the smooth mixed optical case]
\label{prop:first-bombe-reduction-in-the-smooth-mixed-optical-case}
Assume that the first smooth mixed shortlist case of Definition~\ref{def:first-smooth-mixed-shortlist-case} is present and that the structural bombe of Definition~\ref{def:structural-bombe-on-a-reopening-menu} is run on
\[
\mathcal M_0^{\mathrm{mix}}=\{\mu_{\mathrm B},\mu_{\mathrm C},\mu_{\mathrm{BC}},\mu_{\mathrm D}\}.
\]
Assume further that the current residual picture satisfies the following first applied tests:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=2em,label=(\roman*)]
  \item the shortlist remains smooth under the first comparison rerun, so no leading defect/readout irregularity appears;
  \item under pure boundary recalibration, a curvature-type wavelength drift remains that is incompatible with a boundary-only reading;
  \item under pure carrier-profile refinement, a near-uniform offset component remains that is incompatible with a carrier-only reading;
  \item under a mixed boundary/carrier reopening, the residual does not worsen and stays inside the same smooth shortlist class.
\end{enumerate}
Then the bombe already yields the first nontrivial elimination result
\[
\mu_{\mathrm D}\ \text{eliminated},\qquad
\mu_{\mathrm B}\ \text{eliminated},\qquad
\mu_{\mathrm C}\ \text{eliminated},
\]
so that only the mixed surviving branch
\[
\mu_{\mathrm{BC}}
\]
remains admissible at the present coarse reopening depth.
Moreover, if one opens beneath \(\mu_{\mathrm{BC}}\) the first finite submenu
\[
\mathcal M_1(\mu_{\mathrm{BC}})=\{\nu_{\mathrm{B\to C}},\nu_{\mathrm C},\nu_{\mathrm{C+D}}\},
\]
where \(\nu_{\mathrm{B\to C}}\) means ``first remove the boundary offset, then refine the carrier curvature,'' \(\nu_{\mathrm C}\) means ``use curvature refinement alone inside the mixed parent,'' and \(\nu_{\mathrm{C+D}}\) means ``add an early defect/readout patch already at the second stage,'' then the nested bombe may further eliminate
\[
\nu_{\mathrm C}
\]
by persistence of the offset component and
\[
\nu_{\mathrm{C+D}}
\]
by lack of a defect-like trigger, so that the ordered child branch
\[
\nu_{\mathrm{B\to C}}
\]
remains as the first surviving layered refinement path.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Definition~\ref{def:first-smooth-mixed-shortlist-case} fixes exactly the kind of ambiguity for which a bombe is meant: the shortlist is too structured to justify blind search, but still too mixed to justify an immediate unique inverse claim. By assumption~(i), the defect/readout candidate \(\mu_{\mathrm D}\) fails the back-reading filter already at coarse depth, because the current shortlist remains smooth and does not exhibit the localized irregularity that would move defect/readout reopening to the front. By assumption~(ii), the pure boundary candidate \(\mu_{\mathrm B}\) fails the non-worsening/improvement filter: a remaining curvature drift is precisely the sort of residual that the earlier optical back-reading assigns to carrier-shape mismatch rather than to a boundary-only explanation. By assumption~(iii), the pure carrier candidate \(\mu_{\mathrm C}\) fails symmetrically, because a near-uniform offset cannot be absorbed by carrier-shape refinement alone and therefore points back to an unresolved boundary component. By assumption~(iv), the mixed candidate \(\mu_{\mathrm{BC}}\) survives the first bombe pass, since it neither contradicts the mixed back-reading class nor worsens the residual picture.

The nested stage is then immediate from Proposition~\ref{prop:nested-bombe-backtracking-principle}. Inside the surviving mixed parent, the child candidate \(\nu_{\mathrm C}\) again leaves the offset unresolved and is therefore eliminated. The child candidate \(\nu_{\mathrm{C+D}}\) introduces a defect/readout patch without a defect-class trigger in the shortlist and so fails the current low-order admissibility reading. Hence only \(\nu_{\mathrm{B\to C}}\) remains alive. Therefore the bombe has done more than merely rename the ambiguity: it has reduced a four-element coarse menu to one surviving parent and then reduced the first child submenu to one ordered layered path.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[What the bombe already buys in the first mixed optical case]
\label{cor:what-the-bombe-already-buys-in-the-first-mixed-optical-case}
Whenever a later argument in the present v3.24.0 working line reaches the first smooth mixed shortlist case, it is sufficient to read the bombe gain as follows:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=2em,label=(\roman*)]
  \item defect/readout reopening can be postponed rather than opened prematurely;
  \item a false forced choice between pure boundary and pure carrier explanations is avoided;
  \item the coarse reopening ambiguity collapses to one mixed surviving parent branch;
  \item the first deeper refinement may already be ordered as boundary correction before carrier-curvature correction, instead of exploring all second-stage combinations blindly.
\end{enumerate}
Thus the first applied bombe step already converts a vague mixed optical hint into a strictly smaller and ordered refinement problem.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
This is the operational reading of Proposition~\ref{prop:first-bombe-reduction-in-the-smooth-mixed-optical-case}. The proposition shows that the bombe contributes genuine structural work already in the first mixed test case: it eliminates the wrong coarse sectors, preserves the right mixed parent, and imposes an order on the next refinement depth.
\end{proof}


\begin{remark}[Status of the first defect/readout-near refinement step in v3.24]
\label{rem:status-of-the-first-defect-readout-near-refinement-step-in-v324}
