\section{Closure-Liquid Crystal and Holographic Julia Boundary}
\label{sec:closure-liquid-crystal-holographic-julia-boundary}

The present section introduces a cautious re-reading of the current closure architecture in cellular language. It does \emph{not} claim that the framework is literally a condensed-matter crystal. Instead, it proposes one structured pilot in which the same closure-bearing carrier is treated as a bulk order parameter whose visible sectors appear as phase-sensitive ordered domains and whose Julia-type diagnostics are read as boundary holograms of that same order. The point of this re-reading is organizational: it compresses the current OP~3/OP~5 language into one local compatibility / defect-transport / boundary-readout picture without creating a second closure theory.

\begin{definition}[Closure-liquid-crystal cell]
\label{def:closure-liquid-crystal-cell}
A \emph{closure-liquid-crystal cell} is a quintuple
\[
  X=(K,\sigma,\rho,\phi,\delta)
\]
consisting of:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=2em,label=(\roman*)]
  \item a closure-bearing carrier datum $K$;
  \item a shell/refinement datum $\sigma$;
  \item a branch/route datum $\rho$;
  \item a local phase/readout datum $\phi$;
  \item a local defect datum $\delta$.
\end{enumerate}
The intended reading is that $K$ records the bulk carrier order, while $(\sigma,\rho,\phi,\delta)$ records the visible local realization of that order in one readout domain.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Local cell-compatibility equation]
\label{def:local-cell-compatibility-equation}
Let $X_n=(K_n,\sigma_n,\rho_n,\phi_n,\delta_n)$ and
$X_{n+1}=(K_{n+1},\sigma_{n+1},\rho_{n+1},\phi_{n+1},\delta_{n+1})$
be adjacent closure-liquid-crystal cells. Their local compatibility equation is written
\[
  \mathcal C_{\mathrm{cell}}(X_n,X_{n+1})=0
\]
and is required to mean that:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=2em,label=(\roman*)]
  \item the carrier datum remains inside the same closure-bearing class;
  \item the branch/shell transition between the two cells is admissible;
  \item visible readout variation remains at screening level and does not yet generate a genuine shell defect witness.
\end{enumerate}
Thus the equation $\mathcal C_{\mathrm{cell}}=0$ is the local cellular form of admissible OP~3 passage.
\end{definition}

\begin{proposition}[OP~3 cell-compatibility reading]
\label{prop:op3-cell-compatibility-reading}
Let a translated OP~3 shell passage carry a shell admissibility certificate in the sense of Definition~\ref{def:qam-shell-certificate}. Then it determines two adjacent closure-liquid-crystal cells whose local compatibility equation holds:
\[
  \mathcal C_{\mathrm{cell}}(X_n,X_{n+1})=0.
\]
In particular, the current OP~3 certificate package may be read as a local cell-compatibility law on the same closure-bearing carrier medium.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
A shell admissibility certificate records admissible branch passage, shell-admissible refinement, and closure-compatible readout on the translated OP~3 side. By Lemma~\ref{lem:qam-shell-certificate-closure} and Theorem~\ref{thm:qam-op3-shell-closure}, the source state and the branch-shell return state remain in the same closure-bearing class and differ only by an admissible shell passage together with readout-screening data. This is exactly the content encoded by $\mathcal C_{\mathrm{cell}}(X_n,X_{n+1})=0$ in Definition~\ref{def:local-cell-compatibility-equation}.
\end{proof}

\begin{definition}[Defect transport equation]
\label{def:defect-transport-equation}
Let $X_n$ and $X_{n+1}$ be adjacent closure-liquid-crystal cells. Their defect transport equation is written
\[
  \mathcal D_{\mathrm{cell}}(X_n,X_{n+1})\neq 0
\]
whenever the first local failure is no longer merely screening-visible, but appears as a witness-grade or shell-grade obstruction transported across the current channel. The datum $\mathcal D_{\mathrm{cell}}$ is therefore not a second closure criterion; it is the cellular packaging of the first locally non-contractible obstruction.
\end{definition}

\begin{proposition}[OP~5 defect-transport reading]
\label{prop:op5-defect-transport-reading}
Within the current bundled OP~3$\to$OP~5/global channel, witness-grade OP~5 reopening may be read as defect transport on the same closure-liquid-crystal medium: a bundled global pass corresponds to defect-free or defect-screened transport, while a bundled obstruction corresponds to transported or accumulated non-contractible defect data.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
By Theorem~\ref{thm:bundled-op5-diagnostic-theorem}, Theorem~\ref{thm:first-op3-op5-bundled-transfer}, and Theorem~\ref{thm:first-global-compressed-proof-run-through-extracted-global-tools}, the current channel already distinguishes a bundled pass from a bundled obstruction while subordinating packet/phase/epsilon diagnostics to the carrier-level decision. The witness-grade local/global reopening discipline then identifies the precise place where a local obstruction must be reopened rather than screened away. This is exactly the cellular reading of $\mathcal D_{\mathrm{cell}}\neq 0$: a transported or accumulated defect of one and the same carrier medium rather than a second primitive theory beside the closure channel.
\end{proof}

\begin{definition}[Liquid readout domain]
\label{def:liquid-readout-domain}
Fix a distinguished readout regime $f$. A \emph{liquid readout domain} in regime $f$ is a family of closure-liquid-crystal cells whose carrier data lie in one closure-bearing class while their visible shell/phase data realize one coherent readout phase of that same bulk order. Different regimes or sectors may therefore produce different liquid readout domains without changing the underlying carrier datum in the strong closure sense.
\end{definition}

\begin{remark}[Readouts as liquid-crystal domains of one bulk order]
\label{rem:readouts-as-liquid-crystal-domains}
The point of Definition~\ref{def:liquid-readout-domain} is not to introduce a literal condensed-matter ontology. It is to express the present structural reading more economically: the visible sectors are not independent primitive crystals, but phase-sensitive ordered domains of one deeper closure-bearing bulk carrier. This is the cellular version of the readout-relative principle already used throughout the Companion.
\end{remark}

\begin{definition}[Holographic Julia-boundary readout]
\label{def:holographic-julia-boundary-readout}
Let $\{X_n\}_{n\in I}$ be an admissible closure-liquid-crystal configuration along a chosen branch/route family. A \emph{holographic Julia-boundary readout} is a boundary map
\[
  \mathcal H_{\mathrm{J}}(\{X_n\}_{n\in I})
\]
that records the visible boundary pattern produced by the phase-/shell-sensitive readout of the same bulk carrier configuration. The intended output is a Julia-type boundary image, diagnostic strip, or related visual readout.
\end{definition}

\begin{proposition}[Holographic Julia-boundary principle]
\label{prop:holographic-julia-boundary-principle}
The Julia-type diagnostics used in the present Companion may be read as holographic boundary readouts of an underlying closure-liquid-crystal configuration. In particular, they remain diagnostic or screening-level boundary objects: they support the active closure architecture, but they do not create a new independent closure axiom.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
The current document already treats packet-, phase-lock-, epsilon-, and frame-flicker diagnostics as visible readout layers subordinate to the carrier-level and closure-level statements; see Proposition~\ref{prop:packet-phase-epsilon-screening} and Corollary~\ref{cor:flicker-helix-subordination}. The same discipline applies to Julia-type visuals: they belong on the visible boundary-readout side and are informative exactly insofar as they track admissible passage, defect localization, or loss of admissibility in the bulk carrier medium. Hence they may be read holographically without becoming independent closure generators.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[v3.20 pilot status]
\label{rem:v320-pilot-status}
The present section should be read as a first pilot layer for v3.20.0. It upgrades neither the current OP~3/QAM closure package nor the bundled OP~3$\to$OP~5/global chain by new quantitative claims. Its role is organizational: it packages OP~3 as local cell compatibility, OP~5 as defect transport, visible sectors as liquid-crystal domains, Julia-type visuals as holographic boundary readout of one common carrier order, and tests a first addressed role layer in which the 0-band is reserved for primitive ZF$\leftrightarrow$QAM transport strata beneath later derived role families.
\end{remark}

\begin{remark}[Status of the first addressed-role pilot]
\label{rem:status-of-the-first-addressed-role-pilot}
The closure-liquid-crystal pilot already separates carrier, shell/route, visible phase, and local defect roles. The next small but potentially useful architectural step is to add one controlled address layer for these roles. At the present stage this does \emph{not} replace the active tuple predicates or the current theorem chain. It only tests whether a compact address discipline can stabilize later mixed-tensor use and, in particular, whether the leading 0-band may be reserved for primitive transport strata between ZF and QAM.
\end{remark}

\begin{definition}[Base36 alphabet, Q-bytes, and Q-words]
\label{def:base36-alphabet-q-bytes-q-words}
Let
\[
  \Sigma_{36}:=\{0,1,\dots,9, A,\dots, Z\}
\]
be the fixed base36 alphabet. A \emph{Q-byte} is one symbol of $\Sigma_{36}$. A \emph{Q-word} is an ordered pair
\[
  \alpha\beta\in \Sigma_{36}^{2},
\]
written as a two-symbol address. The intended reading is architectural rather than foundational: the first byte marks a role family, while the second byte marks a local subtype or subregister inside that family.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[0-band transport reservation]
\label{def:zero-band-transport-reservation}
The \emph{0-band} is the subset
\[
  \mathcal B_{0}:=\{0\beta:\beta\in \Sigma_{36}\}\subseteq \Sigma_{36}^{2}.
\]
In the present pilot we reserve $\mathcal B_{0}$ for \emph{primitive transport roles} between ZF and QAM. Concretely, the intended uses of 0-band addresses are transport-side roles such as:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=2em,label=(\roman*)]
  \item visible state-surface transport from active tuple syntax to coded object form;
  \item closure-class transport and factor transport;
  \item admissible transport-graph transport;
  \item readout-factor and class-target transport;
  \item OP$\to$QAM translation transport and partial decoding transport;
  \item exposed-payload / kernel-bridge transport;
  \item boundary-readout transport from bulk carrier data to diagnostic boundary views.
\end{enumerate}
Thus the 0-band is treated as a BIOS-like transport substrate beneath later role families rather than as a family of visible physical sectors.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Derived addressed role families]
\label{def:derived-addressed-role-families}
Let $\alpha\in \Sigma_{36}\setminus\{0\}$. The family
\[
  \mathcal B_{\alpha}:=\{\alpha\beta:\beta\in \Sigma_{36}\}
\]
is called a \emph{derived addressed role family}. Its intended meaning is that addresses in $\mathcal B_{\alpha}$ may carry visible carrier, domain, defect, boundary, tensor, or proof-use roles, but only relative to the primitive transport substrate encoded in the corresponding 0-band addresses $0\beta$. In that sense the later addressed families are built above, rather than beside, the primitive transport layer.
\end{definition}

\begin{proposition}[0-band transport-only viability principle]
\label{prop:zero-band-transport-only-viability-principle}
Reserving the entire 0-band for primitive ZF$\leftrightarrow$QAM transport roles is compatible with the present active Companion line and is structurally useful. More precisely:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=2em,label=(\roman*)]
  \item it does not alter any active tuple predicate or active closure theorem, because those remain stated on the visible coded surface;
  \item it is compatible with the current translation/decoding architecture, because the admissible OP fragment, the partial decoding map, closure-compatible readout, and the deferred kernel bridge already distinguish visible coded objects from the transport maps that connect them;
  \item it gives a clean primitive substrate on which later addressed families $\mathcal B_{\alpha}$ can build without forcing a global redesign of the current QAM layer.
\end{enumerate}
Hence the present pilot may consistently treat the 0-band as a pure transport register beneath later derived role families.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Clause (i) is immediate because the active predicates such as $QState$, $QClEq$, $QAdmTransport$, and the branch/shell/routed predicates are not replaced by the address layer; the address layer is only an auxiliary architectural overlay. Clause (ii) follows from the structure already present in the active text: Theorem~\ref{thm:qam-translation} separates admissible OP-side data from their coded QAM image, Definition~\ref{def:partial-decoding-map} and Proposition~\ref{prop:round-trip-property-admissible-fragment} separate the reverse reading map, Definition~\ref{def:qam-closure-compatible-readout} separates closure-compatible readout transport, and the deferred kernel bridge data separate exposed payload transport from visible coded surfaces. Clause (iii) then follows because later addressed role families no longer need their own primitive transport infrastructure: they may inherit it from the reserved 0-band. Thus the 0-band may be read as a BIOS-like transport substrate without disturbing the active theorem surface.
\end{proof}

\begin{definition}[Pilot-admissible mixed addressed crystal tensor]
\label{def:pilot-admissible-mixed-addressed-crystal-tensor}
Let $X_1$ and $X_2$ be closure-liquid-crystal cells carrying addressed roles $\alpha\beta$ and $\gamma\delta$ with $\alpha\neq\gamma$. Their tensor coupling is called \emph{pilot-admissible mixed addressed} if:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=2em,label=(\roman*)]
  \item the corresponding primitive transport words $0\beta$ and $0\delta$ are already active in the 0-band transport layer;
  \item the coupled configuration preserves cell compatibility or defect readability at the active closure level;
  \item the mixed coupling can be read through the inherited 0-band transport substrate instead of forcing a new primitive role family.
\end{enumerate}
This is the first addressed mixed-tensor pilot: mixed tensors are not globally activated, but they may be tested locally whenever their transport support is already registered in the 0-band.
\end{definition}

\begin{remark}[Why the 0-band helps mixed tensors]
\label{rem:why-the-zero-band-helps-mixed-tensors}
The usefulness of the 0-band reservation is that it turns later mixed tensors into controlled role couplings rather than unrestricted new primitives. In particular, carrier--domain, domain--defect, and carrier--boundary couplings may later be tested by asking whether their transport support is already present in $\mathcal B_{0}$. If it is not, the mixed tensor should remain deferred. If it is, the mixed tensor may be read as a derived coupling above the primitive transport substrate.
\end{remark}

\begin{definition}[Pilot carrier--domain addressed tensor]
\label{def:pilot-carrier-domain-addressed-tensor}
Let $X_{\mathrm{car}}$ be a closure-liquid-crystal cell read in a carrier role and let $X_{\mathrm{dom}}$ be a closure-liquid-crystal cell read in a liquid readout-domain role, with addressed words
\[
\operatorname{addr}(X_{\mathrm{car}})=\alpha\beta,\qquad \operatorname{addr}(X_{\mathrm{dom}})=\gamma\delta,\qquad \alpha\neq\gamma.
\]
Their coupling
\[
X_{\mathrm{car}}\otimes X_{\mathrm{dom}}
\]
is called a \emph{pilot carrier--domain addressed tensor} if:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=2em,label=(\roman*)]
  \item the inherited primitive transport words $0\beta$ and $0\delta$ are active in the reserved 0-band;
  \item the carrier role fixes the same closure-bearing bulk order that the domain role reads out visibly;
  \item the coupled tensor is interpreted as one bulk/domain pairing rather than as a second primitive closure carrier.
\end{enumerate}
\end{definition}

\begin{proposition}[First carrier--domain addressed tensor admissibility test]
\label{prop:first-carrier-domain-addressed-tensor-admissibility-test}
Let $X_{\mathrm{car}}$ and $X_{\mathrm{dom}}$ satisfy Definition~\ref{def:pilot-carrier-domain-addressed-tensor}. Assume moreover that the carrier reading is closure-stable and that the domain reading differs from the carrier only by visible shell/readout realization. Then the mixed tensor
\[
X_{\mathrm{car}}\otimes X_{\mathrm{dom}}
\]
is pilot-admissible in the sense of Definition~\ref{def:pilot-admissible-mixed-addressed-crystal-tensor}. In particular, carrier--domain coupling may now be treated as the first concrete locally licensed mixed addressed tensor above the 0-band transport substrate.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
By Definition~\ref{def:pilot-carrier-domain-addressed-tensor}, the primitive transport support of both roles is already present in the reserved 0-band through $0\beta$ and $0\delta$. The standing assumption says that the carrier reading and the domain reading do not introduce two distinct closure carriers: they share one and the same closure-bearing bulk order, while the domain role records only a visible shell/readout realization of that bulk order. Hence the mixed tensor does not force a new primitive role family. Since the coupled object therefore preserves the active closure-bearing content and remains readable through the inherited transport substrate, all three clauses of Definition~\ref{def:pilot-admissible-mixed-addressed-crystal-tensor} hold.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Carrier--domain pilot use rule]
\label{cor:carrier-domain-pilot-use-rule}
Whenever a later argument needs to express that one visible domain is only a readout phase of a closure-stable carrier and the relevant primitive transport support is already active in the 0-band, it may cite Proposition~\ref{prop:first-carrier-domain-addressed-tensor-admissibility-test} and treat the pair as one pilot-admissible mixed addressed tensor. A finer reopening is needed only when the argument depends on defect loading or boundary participation not already encoded by the carrier--domain pairing.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
This is the operational reformulation of Proposition~\ref{prop:first-carrier-domain-addressed-tensor-admissibility-test}. The proposition already isolates the precise point at which carrier and visible domain may be coupled without creating a second primitive closure carrier.
\end{proof}

\begin{definition}[Pilot domain--defect addressed tensor]
\label{def:pilot-domain-defect-addressed-tensor}
Let $X_{\mathrm{dom}}$ be a closure-liquid-crystal cell read in a liquid readout-domain role and let $X_{\mathrm{def}}$ be a closure-liquid-crystal cell read in a defect role, with addressed words
\[
\operatorname{addr}(X_{\mathrm{dom}})=\alpha\beta,\qquad \operatorname{addr}(X_{\mathrm{def}})=\gamma\delta,\qquad \alpha\neq\gamma.
\]
Their coupling
\[
X_{\mathrm{dom}}\otimes X_{\mathrm{def}}
\]
is called a \emph{pilot domain--defect addressed tensor} if:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=2em,label=(\roman*)]
  \item the inherited primitive transport words $0\beta$ and $0\delta$ are active in the reserved 0-band;
  \item the defect role is read as a localized loading, witness, or transported obstruction on the same visible domain rather than as a second independent visible sector;
  \item the coupled tensor preserves the distinction between visible domain content and defect content, so that defect transport is recorded on top of domain visibility instead of collapsing both into one undifferentiated readout.
\end{enumerate}
\end{definition}

\begin{proposition}[First domain--defect addressed tensor admissibility test]
\label{prop:first-domain-defect-addressed-tensor-admissibility-test}
Let $X_{\mathrm{dom}}$ and $X_{\mathrm{def}}$ satisfy Definition~\ref{def:pilot-domain-defect-addressed-tensor}. Assume moreover that the visible domain remains attached to one closure-stable carrier and that the defect role measures only local loading, witness-grade obstruction, or transported mismatch on that same domain. Then the mixed tensor
\[
X_{\mathrm{dom}}\otimes X_{\mathrm{def}}
\]
is pilot-admissible in the sense of Definition~\ref{def:pilot-admissible-mixed-addressed-crystal-tensor}. In particular, domain--defect coupling may now be treated as the second concrete locally licensed mixed addressed tensor above the 0-band transport substrate.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
By Definition~\ref{def:pilot-domain-defect-addressed-tensor}, the primitive transport support of both addressed roles is already present in the reserved 0-band through $0\beta$ and $0\delta$. The standing assumption says that the defect role does not create a second visible bulk or a second primitive closure carrier: it measures only how the already visible domain is loaded, distorted, or obstructed at witness level. Hence the mixed tensor does not force a new primitive role family. Since the visible domain remains attached to one closure-stable carrier while the defect is recorded as added local loading on that same domain, the coupled object preserves active closure-bearing content and remains readable through the inherited transport substrate. Therefore all three clauses of Definition~\ref{def:pilot-admissible-mixed-addressed-crystal-tensor} hold.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Domain--defect pilot use rule]
\label{cor:domain-defect-pilot-use-rule}
Whenever a later argument needs to express that a visible domain carries a local witness, transported defect, or obstruction loading, and whenever the primitive transport support of both roles is already active in the 0-band, it may cite Proposition~\ref{prop:first-domain-defect-addressed-tensor-admissibility-test} and treat the pair as one pilot-admissible mixed addressed tensor. A finer reopening is required only when the argument depends on carrier splitting or boundary participation not already encoded by the domain--defect pairing.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
This is the operational reformulation of Proposition~\ref{prop:first-domain-defect-addressed-tensor-admissibility-test}. The proposition already isolates the precise point at which visible domain and local defect may be coupled without creating a second primitive visible sector.
\end{proof}

\begin{definition}[Pilot carrier--boundary addressed tensor]
\label{def:pilot-carrier-boundary-addressed-tensor}
Let $X_{\mathrm{car}}$ be a closure-liquid-crystal cell read in a carrier role and let $X_{\mathrm{bdy}}$ be a closure-liquid-crystal cell read in a boundary or holographic Julia-boundary role, with addressed words
\[
\operatorname{addr}(X_{\mathrm{car}})=\alpha\beta,\qquad \operatorname{addr}(X_{\mathrm{bdy}})=\gamma\delta,\qquad \alpha\neq\gamma.
\]
Their coupling
\[
X_{\mathrm{car}}\otimes X_{\mathrm{bdy}}
\]
is called a \emph{pilot carrier--boundary addressed tensor} if:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=2em,label=(\roman*)]
  \item the inherited primitive transport words $0\beta$ and $0\delta$ are active in the reserved 0-band;
  \item the boundary role is read as a holographic or projected boundary trace of the same closure-stable carrier rather than as a second independent bulk order;
  \item the coupled tensor records bulk-to-boundary readout without promoting the boundary image to a new primitive carrier family.
\end{enumerate}
\end{definition}

\begin{proposition}[First carrier--boundary addressed tensor admissibility test]
\label{prop:first-carrier-boundary-addressed-tensor-admissibility-test}
Let $X_{\mathrm{car}}$ and $X_{\mathrm{bdy}}$ satisfy Definition~\ref{def:pilot-carrier-boundary-addressed-tensor}. Assume moreover that the carrier reading is closure-stable and that the boundary role is obtained as a holographic Julia-boundary readout of that same carrier, possibly with controlled defect sensitivity but without introducing a second bulk order. Then the mixed tensor
\[
X_{\mathrm{car}}\otimes X_{\mathrm{bdy}}
\]
is pilot-admissible in the sense of Definition~\ref{def:pilot-admissible-mixed-addressed-crystal-tensor}. In particular, carrier--boundary coupling may now be treated as the third concrete locally licensed mixed addressed tensor above the 0-band transport substrate.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
By Definition~\ref{def:pilot-carrier-boundary-addressed-tensor}, the primitive transport support of both addressed roles is already present in the reserved 0-band through $0\beta$ and $0\delta$. The standing assumption says that the boundary role is not a second primitive closure carrier and not an independent bulk order. It is only the holographic or projected boundary trace of the same closure-stable carrier, possibly carrying controlled defect sensitivity in its visible image. Hence the mixed tensor does not force a new primitive role family. Since the coupled object remains readable through the inherited transport substrate and preserves one closure-bearing bulk order with one derived boundary image, all three clauses of Definition~\ref{def:pilot-admissible-mixed-addressed-crystal-tensor} hold.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Carrier--boundary pilot use rule]
\label{cor:carrier-boundary-pilot-use-rule}
Whenever a later argument needs to express that a boundary or Julia-type image is only a holographic readout of a closure-stable carrier and the primitive transport support of both roles is already active in the 0-band, it may cite Proposition~\ref{prop:first-carrier-boundary-addressed-tensor-admissibility-test} and treat the pair as one pilot-admissible mixed addressed tensor. A finer reopening is required only when the argument depends on an additional domain or defect layer not already encoded by the carrier--boundary pairing.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
This is the operational reformulation of Proposition~\ref{prop:first-carrier-boundary-addressed-tensor-admissibility-test}. The proposition already isolates the precise point at which a boundary image may be coupled to a carrier without creating a second primitive bulk order.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[First addressed mixed-tensor pilot triad]
\label{rem:first-addressed-mixed-tensor-pilot-triad}
At the present pilot stage the addressed crystal architecture now supports three locally licensed mixed tensors above the reserved 0-band transport substrate:
\[
\text{carrier--domain},\qquad \text{domain--defect},\qquad \text{carrier--boundary}.
\]
These three are not yet a full mixed-tensor calculus. They are the first controlled test family showing that visible phase, witness loading, and holographic boundary readout may all be coupled to one closure-bearing carrier without forcing new primitive bulk families.
\end{remark}

\begin{remark}[Status of the first bundled addressed mixed-tensor surface]
\label{rem:status-of-the-first-bundled-addressed-mixed-tensor-surface}
The present line still does \emph{not} activate a global mixed-tensor calculus for all addressed crystal roles. What it now does support, however, is one first bundled addressed pilot surface: whenever a later argument uses only the three locally licensed couplings
\[
\text{carrier--domain},\qquad \text{domain--defect},\qquad \text{carrier--boundary},
\]
and all three are read through the inherited reserved 0-band transport substrate, the argument may cite them as one finite addressed pilot package rather than reopen each mixed tensor from scratch.
\end{remark}

\begin{proposition}[First bundled addressed mixed-tensor pilot principle]
\label{prop:first-bundled-addressed-mixed-tensor-pilot-principle}
Assume that a later argument involves only the three locally licensed addressed couplings from Remark~\ref{rem:first-addressed-mixed-tensor-pilot-triad}, namely carrier--domain, domain--defect, and carrier--boundary, and that in each case the relevant primitive transport words remain active in the reserved 0-band. Assume moreover that no step of the argument introduces a second primitive closure-bearing bulk family. Then the whole mixed-tensor part of the argument may be treated as one bundled addressed mixed-tensor pilot package above the 0-band transport substrate. In particular:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=2em,label=(\roman*)]
  \item the visible domain phase may be coupled to the closure-stable carrier without creating a second carrier;
  \item witness-grade or transported defect loading may be read on that same visible domain without creating a second visible sector;
  \item the boundary or Julia-type image may be read as a holographic boundary trace of the same carrier without creating a second bulk order.
\end{enumerate}
Consequently, a later proof using only these three couplings may cite one bundled addressed pilot surface instead of reopening each of the three mixed tensors separately.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
The carrier--domain case is exactly Proposition~\ref{prop:first-carrier-domain-addressed-tensor-admissibility-test}. The domain--defect case is exactly Proposition~\ref{prop:first-domain-defect-addressed-tensor-admissibility-test}. The carrier--boundary case is exactly Proposition~\ref{prop:first-carrier-boundary-addressed-tensor-admissibility-test}. Under the standing assumption that all three inherited primitive transport supports remain active in the reserved 0-band and that no step introduces a second primitive closure-bearing bulk family, the three pilot-admissible mixed tensors sit above the same transport substrate and preserve the same one-bulk reading. Hence they may be cited together as one finite addressed pilot package rather than as three unrelated local exceptions.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Bundled addressed pilot use rule]
\label{cor:bundled-addressed-pilot-use-rule}
Whenever a later argument needs only the combined force of carrier--domain visibility, domain--defect loading, and carrier--boundary readout, and whenever all corresponding primitive transport supports are already active in the 0-band, it is sufficient to cite Proposition~\ref{prop:first-bundled-addressed-mixed-tensor-pilot-principle} and work with one bundled addressed pilot surface. A finer reopening is required only when a later step introduces an additional mixed role family not already contained in the carrier--domain / domain--defect / carrier--boundary triad.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
This is the operational reformulation of Proposition~\ref{prop:first-bundled-addressed-mixed-tensor-pilot-principle}. The proposition already isolates the precise point at which the current three-role pilot family may be treated as one bundled addressed surface and the precise point at which the present pilot compression stops.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Status of the first local addressed crystal-packet step]
\label{rem:status-of-the-first-local-addressed-crystal-packet-step}
The present line still does \emph{not} activate one unrestricted mixed-tensor algebra for all addressed roles. What it now does support, however, is one first local addressed crystal packet: whenever a later argument uses one carrier role together with a visible domain phase, a defect loading on that same visible domain, and a boundary trace of the same carrier, all read through the inherited reserved 0-band transport substrate, the whole quartet may be treated as one local addressed crystal configuration rather than as four unrelated role fragments.
\end{remark}

\begin{definition}[Local addressed crystal packet]
\label{def:local-addressed-crystal-packet}
A \emph{local addressed crystal packet} is a finite addressed role tuple
\[
\Pi_{\mathrm{loc}}=(X_{\mathrm{car}},X_{\mathrm{dom}},X_{\mathrm{def}},X_{\mathrm{bdy}})
\]
such that:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=2em,label=(\roman*)]
  \item the pairs $(X_{\mathrm{car}},X_{\mathrm{dom}})$, $(X_{\mathrm{dom}},X_{\mathrm{def}})$, and $(X_{\mathrm{car}},X_{\mathrm{bdy}})$ are all pilot-admissible mixed addressed tensors in the previously established sense;
  \item all relevant primitive transport words for the addressed roles of the tuple are active in the reserved 0-band;
  \item the visible domain phase, the defect loading, and the boundary trace are all read as derived roles of one and the same closure-stable carrier, not as independent primitive bulk families.
\end{enumerate}
\end{definition}

\begin{proposition}[First local addressed crystal-packet principle]
\label{prop:first-local-addressed-crystal-packet-principle}
Let
\[
\Pi_{\mathrm{loc}}=(X_{\mathrm{car}},X_{\mathrm{dom}},X_{\mathrm{def}},X_{\mathrm{bdy}})
\]
be a local addressed crystal packet in the sense of Definition~\ref{def:local-addressed-crystal-packet}. Then the tuple may be treated as one local crystal configuration with four distinguished role faces:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=2em,label=(\roman*)]
  \item a closure-stable carrier face;
  \item a visible domain face;
  \item a defect or witness-loading face on that same domain;
  \item a holographic boundary face of that same carrier.
\end{enumerate}
In particular, later arguments may cite the packet as one local addressed crystal configuration whenever they need only the joint presence of carrier, visible domain, defect loading, and boundary readout, and do not require a finer reopening of the internal pilot couplings.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
By clause (i) of Definition~\ref{def:local-addressed-crystal-packet}, each of the three required mixed addressed couplings is already pilot-admissible: carrier--domain by Proposition~\ref{prop:first-carrier-domain-addressed-tensor-admissibility-test}, domain--defect by Proposition~\ref{prop:first-domain-defect-addressed-tensor-admissibility-test}, and carrier--boundary by Proposition~\ref{prop:first-carrier-boundary-addressed-tensor-admissibility-test}. By clause (ii), all addressed roles of the tuple inherit their primitive transport support from the same reserved 0-band substrate. By clause (iii), the visible domain, defect loading, and boundary trace are all derived roles of one closure-stable carrier rather than separate primitive bulk families. Therefore the tuple is not merely a list of unrelated addressed roles. It is one local crystal configuration carrying four distinguished faces of the same underlying local closure-bearing order.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Local addressed crystal-packet use rule]
\label{cor:local-addressed-crystal-packet-use-rule}
Whenever a later argument needs only one closure-stable carrier together with its visible domain phase, a defect loading on that domain, and a boundary or Julia-type trace of the same carrier, and whenever all primitive transport supports are already active in the reserved 0-band, it is sufficient to cite Proposition~\ref{prop:first-local-addressed-crystal-packet-principle} and work with one local addressed crystal packet. A finer reopening is required only when the argument depends on an additional role family or on an internal pilot coupling not already encoded by the packet.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
This is the operational reformulation of Proposition~\ref{prop:first-local-addressed-crystal-packet-principle}. The proposition already isolates the precise point at which the four addressed roles may be treated as one local crystal configuration instead of being reopened separately.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Status of the first addressed crystal-corridor step]
\label{rem:status-of-the-first-addressed-crystal-corridor-step}
The present line still does \emph{not} activate one unrestricted global crystal lattice of addressed roles. What it now does support, however, is one first addressed crystal corridor: a finite ordered chain of local addressed crystal packets may be read together whenever they are carried by the same closure-stable carrier line and all role transitions remain supported by the inherited reserved 0-band transport substrate.
\end{remark}

\begin{definition}[Addressed crystal corridor]
\label{def:addressed-crystal-corridor}
An \emph{addressed crystal corridor} is a finite ordered family
\[
\mathfrak C=(\Pi_1,\dots,\Pi_n)
\]
of local addressed crystal packets such that:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=2em,label=(\roman*)]
  \item each $\Pi_k$ is a local addressed crystal packet in the sense of Definition~\ref{def:local-addressed-crystal-packet};
  \item the carrier face of $\Pi_k$ and the carrier face of $\Pi_{k+1}$ are read as successive closure-stable carrier realizations of one and the same transported carrier line;
  \item all domain, defect, and boundary role transitions between neighboring packets remain readable through active primitive transport words in the reserved 0-band;
  \item no packet in the chain forces a second primitive closure-bearing bulk family.
\end{enumerate}
\end{definition}

\begin{proposition}[First addressed crystal-corridor principle]
\label{prop:first-addressed-crystal-corridor-principle}
Let
\[
\mathfrak C=(\Pi_1,\dots,\Pi_n)
\]
be an addressed crystal corridor in the sense of Definition~\ref{def:addressed-crystal-corridor}. Then the whole chain may be treated as one finite carrier-stable local corridor of addressed crystal data. In particular:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=2em,label=(\roman*)]
  \item the carrier faces of the packets define one finite closure-stable carrier corridor;
  \item the visible domain phases form one finite family of derived domain faces along that corridor;
  \item the defect loadings form one finite family of local witness/obstruction faces on the same corridor;
  \item the boundary traces form one finite family of holographic faces of that same corridor.
\end{enumerate}
Consequently, later arguments may cite the whole corridor as one finite addressed crystal corridor whenever they need only the joint local-to-local propagation of carrier, domain, defect, and boundary information and do not require reopening of the internal packet transitions.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
By clause (i) of Definition~\ref{def:addressed-crystal-corridor}, each packet $\Pi_k$ is already a local addressed crystal packet by Proposition~\ref{prop:first-local-addressed-crystal-packet-principle}. Clause (ii) says that the carrier faces of neighboring packets are not unrelated bulk objects but successive realizations of one transported closure-stable carrier line. Clause (iii) says that the visible domain, defect, and boundary transitions between neighboring packets remain readable through the active primitive 0-band transport support. Clause (iv) excludes the appearance of a second primitive closure-bearing bulk family. Hence the chain is not merely a finite list of unrelated local packets: it is one finite corridor of addressed crystal data carried by one closure-stable transport line.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Addressed crystal-corridor use rule]
\label{cor:addressed-crystal-corridor-use-rule}
Whenever a later argument needs only finite local propagation of one closure-stable carrier together with its domain phases, defect loadings, and boundary traces across a sequence of neighboring local packets, and whenever all packet transitions remain supported by the reserved 0-band, it is sufficient to cite Proposition~\ref{prop:first-addressed-crystal-corridor-principle} and work with one addressed crystal corridor. A finer reopening is required only when the argument depends on a packet transition that introduces a new role family or leaves the active 0-band transport substrate.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
This is the operational reformulation of Proposition~\ref{prop:first-addressed-crystal-corridor-principle}. The proposition already isolates the precise point at which a finite chain of local packets may be treated as one carrier-stable local corridor rather than reopened packet by packet.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Status of the first corridor-hologram step]
\label{rem:status-of-the-first-corridor-hologram-step}
The present line still does \emph{not} claim one full global holographic reconstruction theorem for arbitrary addressed crystal data. What it now does support, however, is one first corridor-hologram reading: a finite addressed crystal corridor may be read through one aggregated holographic Julia-boundary profile whenever the whole corridor remains carried by the same closure-stable transport line and all packet-to-packet transitions remain supported by the reserved 0-band.
\end{remark}

\begin{definition}[Corridor holographic Julia profile]
\label{def:corridor-holographic-julia-profile}
Let
\[
\mathfrak C=(\Pi_1,\dots,\Pi_n)
\]
be an addressed crystal corridor in the sense of Definition~\ref{def:addressed-crystal-corridor}. Its \emph{corridor holographic Julia profile}, written
\[
\mathcal H_{\mathrm{corr}}(\mathfrak C),
\]
is the finite boundary-readout object obtained by collecting the boundary faces of the packets $\Pi_k$ along the common carrier corridor and reading them as one ordered holographic boundary profile of the same transported closure-stable carrier line.
\end{definition}

\begin{proposition}[First corridor-hologram principle]
\label{prop:first-corridor-hologram-principle}
Let $\mathfrak C$ be an addressed crystal corridor. Assume that:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=2em,label=(\roman*)]
  \item the carrier corridor remains closure-stable throughout the packets of $\mathfrak C$;
  \item the packet boundary faces are all derived holographic traces of that same carrier corridor;
  \item no packet transition introduces a second primitive closure-bearing bulk family or leaves the active reserved 0-band transport substrate.
\end{enumerate}
Then the boundary contribution of the whole corridor may be treated as one corridor holographic Julia profile
\[
\mathcal H_{\mathrm{corr}}(\mathfrak C)
\]
instead of reopening the packet boundary faces one by one. In particular, finite boundary propagation along the corridor may be cited through one aggregated holographic boundary profile attached to the common carrier corridor.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
By Proposition~\ref{prop:first-addressed-crystal-corridor-principle}, the packets of $\mathfrak C$ already form one finite carrier-stable local corridor of addressed crystal data. Under clause (i), this carrier corridor does not split into unrelated bulk lines. Under clause (ii), each packet boundary face is not an independent primitive bulk object but a derived holographic trace of that same carrier corridor. Under clause (iii), the packet transitions remain readable through the active reserved 0-band and do not force a second primitive closure-bearing bulk family. Hence the ordered family of packet boundary faces may be collected into one aggregated boundary-readout object, namely the corridor holographic Julia profile $\mathcal H_{\mathrm{corr}}(\mathfrak C)$, without reopening the boundary faces separately.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Corridor-hologram use rule]
\label{cor:corridor-hologram-use-rule}
Whenever a later argument needs only the finite holographic boundary propagation of one closure-stable addressed crystal corridor, and whenever all packet transitions remain supported by the reserved 0-band, it is sufficient to cite Proposition~\ref{prop:first-corridor-hologram-principle} and work with the single aggregated boundary object
\[
\mathcal H_{\mathrm{corr}}(\mathfrak C).
\]
A finer reopening is required only when the argument depends on a packet-specific boundary feature not already encoded by the corridor profile.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
This is the operational reformulation of Proposition~\ref{prop:first-corridor-hologram-principle}. The proposition already isolates the precise point at which packetwise boundary traces may be compressed to one corridor-level holographic Julia profile.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Status of the first local-to-boundary crystal-readout compression step]
\label{rem:status-of-the-first-local-to-boundary-crystal-readout-compression-step}
The present line still does \emph{not} identify every addressed crystal corridor with one unrestricted global bulk object. What it now does support, however, is one first local-to-boundary compression step: whenever a finite addressed crystal corridor is carried by one closure-stable carrier line and its visible domain, defect, and boundary faces remain within the active addressed pilot architecture, the whole corridor may be cited through one joint crystal-readout object rather than through separate carrier-, domain-, defect-, and boundary clauses.
\end{remark}

\begin{definition}[Addressed crystal readout profile]
\label{def:addressed-crystal-readout-profile}
Let $\mathfrak C$ be an addressed crystal corridor and let $\mathcal H_{\mathrm{corr}}(\mathfrak C)$ be its corridor holographic Julia profile. The \emph{addressed crystal readout profile} of $\mathfrak C$, written
\[
\mathcal R_{\mathrm{cr}}(\mathfrak C),
\]
is the finite aggregated readout object consisting of:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=2em,label=(\roman*)]
  \item the carrier corridor of $\mathfrak C$ as closure-bearing transport line;
  \item the ordered family of visible domain faces along that corridor;
  \item the ordered family of defect-load faces on those domains;
  \item the corridor holographic Julia profile $\mathcal H_{\mathrm{corr}}(\mathfrak C)$.
\end{enumerate}
Thus $\mathcal R_{\mathrm{cr}}(\mathfrak C)$ records one finite local-to-boundary crystal readout package for the corridor.
\end{definition}

\begin{proposition}[First local-to-boundary crystal-readout compression principle]
\label{prop:first-local-to-boundary-crystal-readout-compression-principle}
Let $\mathfrak C$ be an addressed crystal corridor. Assume that:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=2em,label=(\roman*)]
  \item $\mathfrak C$ satisfies the corridor conditions of Proposition~\ref{prop:first-addressed-crystal-corridor-principle};
  \item its holographic Julia boundary data satisfy Proposition~\ref{prop:first-corridor-hologram-principle};
  \item no step of the corridor leaves the active addressed pilot role families or forces a second primitive closure-bearing bulk family.
\end{enumerate}
Then the full local-to-boundary content of the corridor may be cited by the single addressed crystal readout profile
\[
\mathcal R_{\mathrm{cr}}(\mathfrak C)
\]
instead of reopening separately the carrier corridor, domain faces, defect faces, and boundary profile. In particular, a later proof that needs only the joint propagation of these four layers across the corridor may work with one finite addressed crystal readout package.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
By Proposition~\ref{prop:first-addressed-crystal-corridor-principle}, the packets of $\mathfrak C$ already define one finite carrier-stable corridor together with one ordered family of domain faces and one ordered family of defect-load faces. By Proposition~\ref{prop:first-corridor-hologram-principle}, the packetwise boundary traces of the same corridor already compress to the single aggregated boundary object $\mathcal H_{\mathrm{corr}}(\mathfrak C)$. Assumption (iii) ensures that the whole corridor remains inside the active addressed pilot architecture and does not split into a second primitive closure-bearing bulk family. Hence the four layers belong to one and the same finite corridor package and may be cited through the single readout object $\mathcal R_{\mathrm{cr}}(\mathfrak C)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Local-to-boundary crystal-readout use rule]
\label{cor:local-to-boundary-crystal-readout-use-rule}
Whenever a later argument needs only the finite joint propagation of one closure-stable carrier corridor, its visible domain faces, its defect-load faces, and its holographic Julia-boundary profile, and whenever the whole corridor remains inside the active addressed pilot architecture, it is sufficient to cite Proposition~\ref{prop:first-local-to-boundary-crystal-readout-compression-principle} and work with the single readout object
\[
\mathcal R_{\mathrm{cr}}(\mathfrak C).
\]
A finer reopening is required only when the argument depends on a packet-specific role feature not already encoded by the addressed crystal readout profile.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
This is the operational reformulation of Proposition~\ref{prop:first-local-to-boundary-crystal-readout-compression-principle}. The proposition already isolates the precise point at which the whole finite corridor may be treated as one addressed crystal readout package.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Status of the first addressed crystal-readout class step]
\label{rem:status-of-the-first-addressed-crystal-readout-class-step}
The present line still does \emph{not} identify arbitrary crystal corridors through one unrestricted global quotient. What it now does support, however, is one first addressed crystal-readout class step: whenever two finite addressed crystal corridors carry the same closure-stable carrier line, the same visible domain/defect layering pattern, and the same corridor holographic Julia profile at the active pilot level, they may be treated as belonging to one and the same local-to-boundary readout class.
\end{remark}

\begin{definition}[Addressed crystal-readout class]
\label{def:addressed-crystal-readout-class}
Let $\mathfrak C_1$ and $\mathfrak C_2$ be addressed crystal corridors. We write
\[
\mathfrak C_1 \sim_{\mathrm{cr}} \mathfrak C_2
\]
if the addressed crystal readout profiles
\[
\mathcal R_{\mathrm{cr}}(\mathfrak C_1)
\quad\text{and}\quad
\mathcal R_{\mathrm{cr}}(\mathfrak C_2)
\]
agree at the active pilot level in the following sense:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=2em,label=(\roman*)]
  \item they are carried by the same closure-stable carrier pattern;
  \item they have the same ordered visible domain-face pattern;
  \item they have the same ordered defect-load pattern;
  \item they have the same corridor holographic Julia profile pattern.
\end{enumerate}
The equivalence class of $\mathfrak C$ under this relation is called its \emph{addressed crystal-readout class} and is written
\[
[\mathfrak C]_{\mathrm{cr}}.
\]
\end{definition}

\begin{proposition}[First addressed crystal-readout class principle]
\label{prop:first-addressed-crystal-readout-class-principle}
Let $\mathfrak C_1$ and $\mathfrak C_2$ be addressed crystal corridors with
\[
\mathfrak C_1 \sim_{\mathrm{cr}} \mathfrak C_2.
\]
Then any later argument that depends only on the active local-to-boundary readout content encoded by
\[
\mathcal R_{\mathrm{cr}}(\mathfrak C_1)
\quad\text{or}\quad
\mathcal R_{\mathrm{cr}}(\mathfrak C_2)
\]
may replace either corridor by the same addressed crystal-readout class
\[
[\mathfrak C_1]_{\mathrm{cr}}=[\mathfrak C_2]_{\mathrm{cr}}.
\]
In particular, once a proof uses only carrier corridor, domain-face pattern, defect-load pattern, and corridor holographic profile at the active pilot level, it need not distinguish between corridors lying in the same addressed crystal-readout class.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
By Definition~\ref{def:addressed-crystal-readout-class}, the equivalence relation $\sim_{\mathrm{cr}}$ is imposed exactly by agreement of the active pilot data already collected in the addressed crystal readout profile. Therefore two equivalent corridors do not differ at the level of carrier pattern, domain-face pattern, defect-load pattern, or corridor holographic Julia profile. But Proposition~\ref{prop:first-local-to-boundary-crystal-readout-compression-principle} says that these four layers are precisely the whole active local-to-boundary readout content currently retained. Hence a later argument depending only on that active content cannot distinguish two corridors in the same class.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Addressed crystal-readout class use rule]
\label{cor:addressed-crystal-readout-class-use-rule}
Whenever a later argument needs only the active local-to-boundary readout content of an addressed crystal corridor, it is sufficient to cite Proposition~\ref{prop:first-addressed-crystal-readout-class-principle} and work with the class
\[
[\mathfrak C]_{\mathrm{cr}}
\]
instead of a chosen corridor representative. A finer reopening is required only when the argument depends on corridor-internal data not already encoded by the addressed crystal readout profile.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
This is the operational reformulation of Proposition~\ref{prop:first-addressed-crystal-readout-class-principle}. The proposition already isolates the precise point at which one may pass from a concrete addressed crystal corridor to its local-to-boundary readout class.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Status of the first addressed crystal-readout class composition step]
\label{rem:status-of-the-first-addressed-crystal-readout-class-composition-step}
The present line still does \emph{not} claim one unrestricted global algebra of crystal-readout classes. What it now does support, however, is one first local composition rule: whenever two finite addressed crystal corridors meet along the same closure-stable carrier pattern and their active local-to-boundary readout classes agree at the shared interface, the two classes may be composed into one larger finite readout class without reopening the corridor representatives.
\end{remark}

\begin{definition}[Composable addressed crystal-readout classes]
\label{def:composable-addressed-crystal-readout-classes}
Let $[\mathfrak C_1]_{\mathrm{cr}}$ and $[\mathfrak C_2]_{\mathrm{cr}}$ be addressed crystal-readout classes. They are called \emph{composable} if there exist representatives $\mathfrak C_1$ and $\mathfrak C_2$ such that:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=2em,label=(\roman*)]
  \item the terminal carrier pattern of $\mathfrak C_1$ agrees with the initial carrier pattern of $\mathfrak C_2$;
  \item the terminal visible domain/defect/boundary pattern of $\mathfrak C_1$ agrees with the initial visible domain/defect/boundary pattern of $\mathfrak C_2$ at the active pilot level;
  \item the concatenated corridor remains inside the active addressed pilot architecture and does not introduce a second primitive closure-bearing bulk family.
\end{enumerate}
In that case the composed class is denoted
\[
[\mathfrak C_1]_{\mathrm{cr}} \star_{\mathrm{cr}} [\mathfrak C_2]_{\mathrm{cr}}.
\]
\end{definition}

\begin{proposition}[First addressed crystal-readout class composition principle]
\label{prop:first-addressed-crystal-readout-class-composition-principle}
Let $[\mathfrak C_1]_{\mathrm{cr}}$ and $[\mathfrak C_2]_{\mathrm{cr}}$ be composable addressed crystal-readout classes in the sense of Definition~\ref{def:composable-addressed-crystal-readout-classes}. Then:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=2em,label=(\roman*)]
  \item the composed object
  \[
  [\mathfrak C_1]_{\mathrm{cr}} \star_{\mathrm{cr}} [\mathfrak C_2]_{\mathrm{cr}}
  \]
  is well-defined at the active pilot level, independent of the chosen composable representatives;
  \item it may be read as the addressed crystal-readout class of the concatenated finite corridor;
  \item later arguments depending only on the active local-to-boundary readout content of the concatenated corridor may cite the composed class instead of reopening the two corridor representatives separately.
\end{enumerate}
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
By Definition~\ref{def:composable-addressed-crystal-readout-classes}, there exist representatives $\mathfrak C_1$ and $\mathfrak C_2$ whose carrier, domain, defect, and boundary data agree at the shared interface at the active pilot level. Because each corridor is already controlled only through its addressed crystal-readout class by Proposition~\ref{prop:first-addressed-crystal-readout-class-principle}, changing representatives inside the same classes does not alter that active interface data. Hence the concatenated corridor has the same active local-to-boundary readout content for every choice of composable representatives. Therefore the composed object is well-defined at the class level and may be used in place of the two separate corridor representatives whenever no finer internal reopening is needed.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Addressed crystal-readout class composition use rule]
\label{cor:addressed-crystal-readout-class-composition-use-rule}
Whenever a later argument traverses two neighboring finite addressed crystal corridors whose active readout classes are composable, it is sufficient to cite Proposition~\ref{prop:first-addressed-crystal-readout-class-composition-principle} and work with the single composed class
\[
[\mathfrak C_1]_{\mathrm{cr}} \star_{\mathrm{cr}} [\mathfrak C_2]_{\mathrm{cr}}.
\]
A finer reopening is required only when the argument depends on interface data not already retained by the active local-to-boundary readout classes.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
This is the operational reformulation of Proposition~\ref{prop:first-addressed-crystal-readout-class-composition-principle}. The proposition already isolates the precise point at which two neighboring corridor classes may be replaced by one composed class at the active pilot level.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Status of the first associative addressed crystal-readout class normal-form step]
\label{rem:status-of-the-first-associative-addressed-crystal-readout-class-normal-form-step}
The present line still does \emph{not} claim one unrestricted global semigroup or category of addressed crystal-readout classes. What it now does support, however, is one first associative class-normal-form discipline: a finite ordered chain of composable addressed crystal-readout classes may be read through one parenthesization-independent composed class as long as all intermediate interfaces remain inside the active pilot architecture.
\end{remark}

\begin{definition}[Associative addressed crystal-readout class normal form]
\label{def:associative-addressed-crystal-readout-class-normal-form}
Let
\[
[\mathfrak C_1]_{\mathrm{cr}},\dots,[\mathfrak C_n]_{\mathrm{cr}}
\]
be a finite ordered family of pairwise composable addressed crystal-readout classes. Their \emph{associative addressed crystal-readout class normal form} is the class, written
\[
[\mathfrak C_1,\dots,\mathfrak C_n]_{\star_{\mathrm{cr}}\mathrm{NF}},
\]
obtained by composing the classes along the active pilot interfaces and identifying all parenthesizations that yield the same active carrier/domain/defect/boundary readout content.
\end{definition}

\begin{proposition}[First associative addressed crystal-readout class normal-form principle]
\label{prop:first-associative-addressed-crystal-readout-class-normal-form-principle}
Let
\[
[\mathfrak C_1]_{\mathrm{cr}},\dots,[\mathfrak C_n]_{\mathrm{cr}}
\]
be a finite ordered family of composable addressed crystal-readout classes. Assume that every intermediate interface remains inside the active addressed pilot architecture and does not introduce a second primitive closure-bearing bulk family. Then:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=2em,label=(\roman*)]
  \item the associative normal-form class
  \[
  [\mathfrak C_1,\dots,\mathfrak C_n]_{\star_{\mathrm{cr}}\mathrm{NF}}
  \]
  is well-defined at the active pilot level and independent of parenthesization;
  \item it may be read as the active composed class of the whole finite corridor chain;
  \item later arguments depending only on the active local-to-boundary readout content of the finite chain may cite this single associative normal-form class instead of reopening the intermediate class compositions separately.
\end{enumerate}
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
By Proposition~\ref{prop:first-addressed-crystal-readout-class-composition-principle}, every neighboring pair of composable classes may already be composed at the active pilot level. The standing assumption ensures that each intermediate composition remains inside the same active pilot architecture and does not create a second primitive closure-bearing bulk family. Therefore every parenthesization produces the same active carrier/domain/defect/boundary readout content for the finite chain. Hence the composed class is well-defined independently of parenthesization and may serve as one associative normal-form class for the entire chain.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Associative addressed crystal-readout class normal-form use rule]
\label{cor:associative-addressed-crystal-readout-class-normal-form-use-rule}
Whenever a later argument traverses a finite ordered chain of composable addressed crystal-readout classes and uses only the active local-to-boundary readout content of that chain, it is sufficient to cite Proposition~\ref{prop:first-associative-addressed-crystal-readout-class-normal-form-principle} and work with the single associative class
\[
[\mathfrak C_1,\dots,\mathfrak C_n]_{\star_{\mathrm{cr}}\mathrm{NF}}.
\]
A finer reopening is required only when the argument depends on interface-specific data not already retained by the active class-normal-form quotient.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
This is the operational reformulation of Proposition~\ref{prop:first-associative-addressed-crystal-readout-class-normal-form-principle}. The proposition already isolates the precise point at which a finite ordered chain of composable addressed crystal-readout classes may be replaced by one parenthesization-independent active class.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Status of the first contraction-stable addressed crystal-readout class normal-form step]
\label{rem:status-of-the-first-contraction-stable-addressed-crystal-readout-class-normal-form-step}
The present line still does \emph{not} identify arbitrary corridor chains by one unrestricted global quotient. What it now does support, however, is one first contraction-stable class-normal-form discipline: once a finite ordered chain of composable addressed crystal-readout classes has been compressed to its associative active class, repeated neutral corridor interfaces that do not change the retained carrier/domain/defect/boundary readout content may be contracted away.
\end{remark}

\begin{definition}[Contraction-stable addressed crystal-readout class normal form]
\label{def:contraction-stable-addressed-crystal-readout-class-normal-form}
Let
\[
[\mathfrak C_1,\dots,\mathfrak C_n]_{\star_{\mathrm{cr}}\mathrm{NF}}
\]
be an associative addressed crystal-readout class normal form. Its \emph{contraction-stable addressed crystal-readout class normal form}, written
\[
[\mathfrak C_1,\dots,\mathfrak C_n]_{\star_{\mathrm{cr}}\mathrm{CNF}},
\]
is obtained by contracting every repeated neutral corridor interface that preserves the same active carrier pattern, the same visible domain pattern, the same defect-load pattern, and the same corridor holographic boundary profile at the shared interface. Thus the compressed class retains only the nonredundant active local-to-boundary interfaces.
\end{definition}

\begin{proposition}[First contraction-stable addressed crystal-readout class normal-form principle]
\label{prop:first-contraction-stable-addressed-crystal-readout-class-normal-form-principle}
Let
\[
[\mathfrak C_1,\dots,\mathfrak C_n]_{\star_{\mathrm{cr}}\mathrm{NF}}
\]
be an associative addressed crystal-readout class normal form. Assume that every repeated corridor interface to be contracted preserves the same active carrier/domain/defect/boundary readout data and does not introduce a second primitive closure-bearing bulk family. Then:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=2em,label=(\roman*)]
  \item the contraction-stable class
  \[
  [\mathfrak C_1,\dots,\mathfrak C_n]_{\star_{\mathrm{cr}}\mathrm{CNF}}
  \]
  is well-defined at the active pilot level;
  \item it retains the same active local-to-boundary readout content as the associative class-normal form, except that redundant repeated neutral interfaces are removed;
  \item later arguments depending only on that active local-to-boundary content may cite the contraction-stable class instead of reopening the original associative class-normal form.
\end{enumerate}
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
By Proposition~\ref{prop:first-associative-addressed-crystal-readout-class-normal-form-principle}, the ordered chain already has a well-defined parenthesization-independent active class. The standing assumption says that the interfaces being contracted do not alter the retained carrier pattern, visible domain pattern, defect-load pattern, or holographic boundary profile. Therefore removing such repeated neutral interfaces does not change the active local-to-boundary readout content that the quotient keeps. Since no contracted step introduces a second primitive closure-bearing bulk family, the contracted class remains inside the same active pilot architecture. Hence the contraction-stable class is well-defined and may replace the longer associative class-normal form whenever no finer reopening is needed.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Contraction-stable addressed crystal-readout class normal-form use rule]
\label{cor:contraction-stable-addressed-crystal-readout-class-normal-form-use-rule}
Whenever a later argument uses only the active local-to-boundary readout content of a finite chain of composable addressed crystal-readout classes and repeated neutral corridor interfaces occur, it is sufficient to cite Proposition~\ref{prop:first-contraction-stable-addressed-crystal-readout-class-normal-form-principle} and work with the single contraction-stable class
\[
[\mathfrak C_1,\dots,\mathfrak C_n]_{\star_{\mathrm{cr}}\mathrm{CNF}}.
\]
A finer reopening is required only when the argument depends on interface-specific data not already retained after contraction.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
This is the operational reformulation of Proposition~\ref{prop:first-contraction-stable-addressed-crystal-readout-class-normal-form-principle}. The proposition already isolates the precise point at which repeated neutral corridor interfaces may be removed without changing the active local-to-boundary readout content.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Status of the terminal addressed crystal-readout surface in the present public v3.21.0 release line]
\label{rem:status-of-the-terminal-addressed-crystal-readout-surface-in-the-present-v320-line}
The present line still does \emph{not} claim one unrestricted global crystal-readout theory for all addressed role families. What it now does support, however, is one terminal active surface for the present v3.21.0 working crystal language: whenever a later argument uses only the active local-to-boundary content retained after passage to the contraction-stable addressed crystal-readout class normal form, that contraction-stable class may be treated as the terminal citation object of the present line.
\end{remark}

\begin{proposition}[Terminal citation rule for the present addressed crystal-readout line]
\label{prop:terminal-citation-rule-for-the-present-addressed-crystal-readout-line}
Let
\[
[\mathfrak C_1,\dots,\mathfrak C_n]_{\star_{\mathrm{cr}}\mathrm{CNF}}
\]
be a contraction-stable addressed crystal-readout class normal form. Assume that a later argument depends only on the following active local-to-boundary data retained by that class:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=2em,label=(\roman*)]
  \item the closure-stable carrier pattern;
  \item the visible domain-face pattern;
  \item the defect-load pattern;
  \item the retained holographic boundary profile;
  \item the nonredundant corridor interfaces surviving contraction.
\end{enumerate}
Then the argument may cite the single class
\[
[\mathfrak C_1,\dots,\mathfrak C_n]_{\star_{\mathrm{cr}}\mathrm{CNF}}
\]
as the terminal active object of the present v3.21.0 crystal-readout line and need not reopen any earlier packet-, corridor-, class-composition-, or associative-class stages.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
By Proposition~\ref{prop:first-contraction-stable-addressed-crystal-readout-class-normal-form-principle}, the class
\[
[\mathfrak C_1,\dots,\mathfrak C_n]_{\star_{\mathrm{cr}}\mathrm{CNF}}
\]
already retains exactly the active local-to-boundary readout content of the finite chain after repeated neutral interfaces have been removed. Earlier stages of the present line --- local packets, addressed corridors, corridor holographic profiles, addressed crystal readout profiles, readout classes, class composition, and associative class-normal forms --- were introduced only to justify passage to this contraction-stable class. Therefore, once a later argument depends only on the retained carrier/domain/defect/boundary data listed above, there is no further need to reopen those earlier stages. The contraction-stable class is then the terminal active citation object of the present line.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Operational mini-checklist for the terminal addressed crystal-readout surface]
\label{cor:operational-mini-checklist-for-the-terminal-addressed-crystal-readout-surface}
A later argument may stay entirely on the terminal addressed crystal-readout surface if all of the following are true:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=2em,label=(\roman*)]
  \item it needs only one closure-stable carried crystal line;
  \item it needs only the active visible domain-face pattern along that line;
  \item it needs only the active defect-load pattern along that line;
  \item it needs only the retained holographic boundary profile;
  \item it does not require any packet-specific, corridor-interface-specific, or pre-contraction local role feature that has been forgotten by passage to
  \[
  [\mathfrak C_1,\dots,\mathfrak C_n]_{\star_{\mathrm{cr}}\mathrm{CNF}}.
  \]
\end{enumerate}
If any one of these clauses fails, the proof should reopen the earliest stage at which the missing information is still visible.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
This is the operational reformulation of Proposition~\ref{prop:terminal-citation-rule-for-the-present-addressed-crystal-readout-line}. The proposition identifies the terminal active citation object; the checklist simply states when remaining on that terminal surface is safe and when one must reopen an earlier stage of the crystal-readout construction.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Closed antisymmetry of deficiency elements]
\label{lem:closed-deficiency-antisymmetry}
Let $f$ be a deficiency element in the relevant HC/closure test sector. If the
$J$-symmetric subspace is already essentially self-adjoint on the admissible
core, then the $J$-symmetric part of $f$ vanishes. Equivalently,
\[
  f=f^-\qquad\text{and hence}\qquad Jf=-f.
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Write
\[
  f=f^+ + f^-,\qquad f^+=\tfrac12(f+Jf),\qquad f^- = \tfrac12(f-Jf).
\]
By construction, $f^+$ lies in the $J$-symmetric sector. The repaired Section 12
argument shows that once the admissible $J$-symmetric core is already
essentially self-adjoint, a deficiency element cannot retain a nonzero
$J$-symmetric component. Otherwise one would obtain a nontrivial deficiency
vector in the symmetric core itself, contradicting essential self-adjointness.
Hence $f^+=0$, so $f=f^-$ and therefore $Jf=-f$.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Functional annihilation of deficiency elements by HC]
\label{prop:functional-hc-annihilation}
For every deficiency element $f$ in the closed HC test sector, the compensator
annihilates $f$ at the function level:
\[
  C(f)=\tfrac12(f+Jf)=0.
\]
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
By Lemma~\ref{lem:closed-deficiency-antisymmetry}, every such deficiency element
satisfies $Jf=-f$. Substituting into the defining compensator formula gives
\[
  C(f)=\tfrac12(f+Jf)=\tfrac12(f-f)=0.
\]
So the annihilation is a genuine functional consequence of closed
$J$-antisymmetry, not merely a heuristic tensor slogan.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Tensor representations are secondary to the functional proof]
\label{rem:tensor-secondary-functional-proof}
Any tensor or matrix representative of the compensator is basis-dependent and
should be read only as a representation of the already established function-level
map. In particular, the annihilation of deficiency elements is proved by the
closed antisymmetry route
\[
  f^+=0 \Longrightarrow Jf=-f \Longrightarrow C(f)=0,
\]
not by a standalone coefficient-level matrix argument.
\end{remark}

\begin{lemma}[Anchor-compatibility lemma]
\label{lem:anchor-compatibility-lemma}
Compensator action is compatible with the orthogonal anchor. In particular, HC
stabilizes the admissible readout channel without destroying the distinction
between the anchored third direction and the first two sectors.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
By Lemma~\ref{lem:orthogonal-anchor-lemma}, the third sector is not decorative
but the stabilizing orthogonal anchor. By Theorem~\ref{thm:hc-forcing-theorem},
HC is the mechanism that re-identifies shifted descriptions in a common output
channel. If HC destroyed the anchor distinction, then the stabilized output
would collapse back into an undifferentiated binary pairing and the role of the
third direction would be lost. That would contradict triolic minimality and the
very need for an orthogonal anchor. Therefore HC must act compatibly with the
anchored triolic organization.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Closure forcing lemma]
\label{lem:closure-forcing-lemma}
A triolic state with orthogonal anchor and forced HC is closure-stable.
Equivalently,
\[
\mathrm{Triolic}(x)\wedge \mathrm{Anchored}(x)\wedge \mathrm{HCForced}(x)
\Longrightarrow \mathrm{ClosureStable}(x).
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
We verify the three contributing conditions and their combination.

\smallskip
\noindent\textbf{Step 1: Triolic structure.}
By Lemma~\ref{lem:triolic-minimality-lemma}, a triolic state carries a
three-sector organization $(K_1,K_2,K_3)$ as the minimal nondegenerate
structure compatible with compensator action and closure readout.
In particular, there exists a distinguished third sector $K_3$ in which
the compensator-selected output can be stabilized.

\smallskip
\noindent\textbf{Step 2: Orthogonal anchor.}
By Lemma~\ref{lem:orthogonal-anchor-lemma}, the third sector satisfies
$K_3\perp K_1$ and $K_3\perp K_2$, preventing $K_3$ from being
relabeled or absorbed into the dual pair $(K_1,K_2)$.
The anchor fixes the admissible direction of collapse/light selection.

\smallskip
\noindent\textbf{Step 3: HC forcing.}
By Lemma~\ref{lem:hc-admissibility-lemma}, the compensator-normalized
image $C(x)$ is admissible whenever $x$ is admissible. Since
$\mathrm{HCForced}(x)$ holds, the state lies in the compensator-selected
channel, so $\mathcal{C}x = C(x)$.

\smallskip
\noindent\textbf{Step 4: Closure stability.}
By the semantic--tensor correspondence of
Remark~\ref{rem:semantic-tensor-correspondence},
$\mathrm{ClosureStable}(x)$ is equivalent to
$\hat{K}(\mathcal{C}x) = \mathcal{C}x$.
By Step~3, $\mathcal{C}x = C(x)$, and by the idempotence of $C$
(Lemma~\ref{lem:hc-idempotence-lemma}), $C(C(x))=C(x)$, so $C(x)$
already lies in $\mathrm{im}(C)$.
By Steps~1--2 and Theorem~\ref{thm:fractal} ($\hat{K}(L_n)=L_{n-1}$,
terminating at $S_0$), the anchor fixes $K_3$ as the structural ground
sector; $\mathcal{C}x\in\mathrm{im}(C)$ lies in the $K_3$-aligned
closure-stable class and is therefore a fixpoint of $\hat{K}$ on that
class. Hence $\hat{K}(\mathcal{C}x)=\mathcal{C}x$, i.e.\ $\mathrm{ClosureStable}(x)$. \qed
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Closure-stable iff compensator image]
\label{lem:closure-stable-iff-im-C}
Under the hypotheses of the normalized semantic kernel
(Definition~\ref{def:semantic-structural-kernel}), the following are equivalent
for any admissible state $x$:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
  \item $\mathrm{ClosureStable}(x)$, i.e.\ $\hat{K}(\mathcal{C}x)=\mathcal{C}x$;
  \item $x \in \mathrm{im}(C)$, i.e.\ $\mathcal{C}x = x$.
\end{enumerate}
Hence $\mathrm{im}(C) = \mathcal{S}_0 := \{x \in \mathcal{S} :
\mathrm{ClosureStable}(x)\}$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
\textbf{(ii) $\Rightarrow$ (i).}
Suppose $\mathcal{C}x = x$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:hc-idempotence-lemma},
$C^2 = C$, so $x \in \mathrm{im}(C)$ implies $\mathcal{C}x = x$.
By the ground-state terminality condition (S2) of
Definition~\ref{def:semantic-structural-kernel},
$\hat{K}(x) = x$ for all $x \in S_0$, the photon ground sector.
Since $\mathrm{im}(C)$ is mapped by $\hat{K}$ to the ground sector
(Theorem~\ref{thm:fractal}: $\hat{K}(L_n) = L_{n-1}$, terminating at
$S_0$), and since $\mathcal{C}x = x$ means $x$ is already in the
compensator-selected ground sector, we get $\hat{K}(\mathcal{C}x) =
\hat{K}(x) = x = \mathcal{C}x$. Hence $\mathrm{ClosureStable}(x)$.

\smallskip
\textbf{(i) $\Rightarrow$ (ii).}
Suppose $\hat{K}(\mathcal{C}x) = \mathcal{C}x$, i.e.\ $\mathcal{C}x$ is a fixpoint of $\hat{K}$.
By Theorem~\ref{thm:fractal}, the only fixpoints of $\hat{K}$ in the
cascade are the elements of the ground sector $S_0 = L =
\bigcap_{n\ge 0} L_n$. Hence $\mathcal{C}x \in S_0$.
By the semantic--tensor correspondence
(Remark~\ref{rem:semantic-tensor-correspondence}),
$\mathcal{C}x \in S_0$ is precisely the condition that $\mathcal{C}$
has already reached its fixpoint on $x$, i.e.\ $\mathcal{C}(\mathcal{C}x)
= \mathcal{C}x$. Since $C^2 = C$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:hc-idempotence-lemma}),
this means $\mathcal{C}x \in \mathrm{im}(C)$, but also that $x$ itself
is mapped to the same compensator-fixed point. The re-identification
mechanism (Theorem~\ref{thm:hc-forcing-theorem}) selects precisely those
$x$ for which the compensated image is the state itself in the ground
sector: $\mathcal{C}x = x$. Hence $x \in \mathrm{im}(C)$.

\smallskip
\textbf{Conclusion.}
Both directions hold, so $\mathrm{ClosureStable}(x) \Leftrightarrow
x \in \mathrm{im}(C)$, giving $\mathcal{S}_0 = \mathrm{im}(C)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Closure class proposition]
\label{prop:closure-class-proposition}
The closure-stable states form a structurally distinguished admissibility class.
In particular, closure-stability is not an accidental property of isolated
examples but a reusable criterion for admissible dynamics and readout.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
By Lemma~\ref{lem:closure-forcing-lemma}, closure-stability follows from a fixed
combination of generative conditions rather than from a one-off construction.
By Lemma~\ref{lem:hc-admissibility-lemma}, the relevant states remain inside the
admissible body under compensator normalization, and by
Lemma~\ref{lem:anchor-compatibility-lemma} this process respects the stabilizing
triolic organization. Hence closure-stability is preserved under the normalized
structural mechanism and can be used as a class criterion.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Exact closure criterion]
\label{prop:exact-closure-criterion}
Exact closure is the regime in which the admissible channel selected by HC is
already terminal with respect to the relevant closure test, so that no further
residual compensator correction is required.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
By Lemma~\ref{lem:hc-idempotence-lemma}, compensator-normalized states do not
drift under repeated HC action. Exact closure is therefore the stronger case in
which the normalized state is not merely admissible but already stable under the
relevant closure readout. In the tensor realization this corresponds to the
absence of further leakage from the selected sector into a complementary block;
semantically it means that the compensator-selected channel has already reached
its terminal closure form.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Closure residue lemma]
\label{lem:closure-residue-lemma}
Whenever exact closure fails, the failure can be measured by a residual term
that records the remaining mismatch between HC-normalized admissibility and full
closure stability.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The exact-closure regime of
Proposition~\ref{prop:exact-closure-criterion} is defined precisely by the
absence of further correction after compensator normalization. If this stronger
condition fails while admissibility is still preserved, then there remains a
